speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. On behalf of the Government I would like to welcome all Hon. Members back and to extend our best wishes to you, Sir. I observe from your opening comments that you are in your usual good humour. I think that will have a major
bearing upon the proceedings of the House during the next while.
There have been short preliminary discussions pertaining to the notice of Ways and Means motion which the Hon. Minister of International Trade (Miss Carney) has just laid upon the table. The Bill is printed and ready for introduction. I am advised that the Bill is identical to the Ways and Means motion. We would be prepared to deal with this issue later this day. However, as you and Hon. Members know, Sir, this would require unanimous consent. I would not expect to receive an immediate response from the Opposition House Leaders, but I invite them to consider the matter. Perhaps they may want to advise us of their decision later this day.
A debate on this issue could take place at 3 o'clock this afternoon, or even at 6 o'clock inasmuch as we are on extended hours today, tomorrow and Thursday. I make that proposition to Hon. Members opposite. We are certainly prepared to try to work out arrangements which would be satisfactory to all.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we, of course, have not seen the Ways and Means motion on which the Bill is based. It will be understood that we will have to reserve our position until we have had an opportunity to study the motion. This is a very serious and complex matter. We will be willing to consider the proposal of the Government House Leader, but in view of our opposition to the course of action undertaken by the Government on softwood lumber as represented by the Ways and Means motion, we will have to give careful thought to the best way to deal with this.
While I reciprocate in one way the Government House Leader's wishes for the new year, I can only repeat the saying of an oriental culture, that it is either a blessing or a curse to extend the wish to people that they live in interesting times. I am sure we have begun another stage in that regard. To answer the question about how interesting they will be, we will have to consider the Government House Leader's proposal in light of our own assessment of the Ways and Means motion. I will get back to him on this as soon as possible later this day.

Mr. Speaker, there were both formal and informal discussions earlier today. subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 29 TRADE-PROPOSED EXPORT TAX ON CANADIAN SOFTWOOD LUMBER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 29 I ask leave to move a motion to adjourn the House for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely, the signing and implementing of an agreement with the United States to impose a 15 per cent export tax on certain Canadian softwood lumber products being shipped to the United States.
This agreement deprives the Canadian industry of up to $600 million annually, throws thousands of forestry workers out of work, imperils Canadian sovereignty, allows the U.S. Government the power to veto actions of the federal and provincial levels of Government to assist Canadians in the industry, thereby invading our sovereignty, imposes a retroactive tax on Canadians without parliamentary approval, or even parliamentary debate, and sets an unwelcome and dangerous precedent on Canada's ability to establish its own natural resource policy and its own export potential.

I advise Hon. Members that I have received notice of the application that has just been made to the Chamber by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner). I have also received an application for an emergency debate on the same subject matter.
I think that the Hon. Member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Corbett) wishes to make some comments, and I welcome those comments at this time.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 29 TRADE-PROPOSED EXPORT TAX ON CANADIAN SOFTWOOD LUMBER
speechtext:
I was delighted this morning to hear the Government make the offer of introducing the legislation at the earliest possible convenience. I was also pleased to hear the response from the NDP that they were in agreement with that. I also hope that the Liberals will give their consideration to that offer by the Government. If debate is entered into today on the Bill, this would make my application redundant. I will await your decision, and the decision of the Official Opposition.
My request under Standing Order 29 is based on the recent decision to impose a 15 per cent export tax on softwood lumber which has caused grave concern among Maritime lumber producers. Many producers fear for the economic viability of their operations, and the jobs dependent upon their competitiveness.
The agreement imposes the tax upon all but five Maritime softwood producers that previously enjoyed exemptions from such action. The consequence of such a decision creates a situation whereby the livelihood of Maritime softwood producers is threatened by an action designed to resolve a problem created by extremely low stumpage fees in British Columbia, Alberta, Ontario, and Quebec.
Many lumber producers fear that they will not survive if they are required to pay not only the highest stumpage fees in Canada, but also an additional 15 per cent tax on their exported products. There is also a very real concern that the lumber market within the Maritime provinces may be swamped by western lumber seeking refuge from the tax.

At that time Members of this House were proceeding, in accordance with the desire of His Honour, the Deputy Excellency the Governor General, from the Commons to the Senate Chamber to witness the Royal Assent to Bills. The traditional and solemn procession was invaded by TV cameras and boom microphones. I believe at the time they were after the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski). The operators literally became part of the procession. Because many of

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH

speechtext: The House resumed from December 19, 1986, consideration of the motion of Mr. Crosbie (St. John's West) that Bill C-18, an Act respecting national transportation, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today the House is about to continue debate on Bill C-18, also known as the National Transportation Act, 1986. The purpose of this Bill is to revise the existing National Transportation Act introduced by the Hon. Jack Pickersgill in 1967, legislation that has served the Canadian economy very well during the past twenty years.
Now, it is perfectly normal to want to make certain changes to improve a piece of legislation, but this attempt by the government to turn the whole legislation upside down and

January 19, 1987
National Transportation Act, 1986
question every single aspect in the transportation sector is quite frankly nothing short of absurd. The previous Government admitted there was a case for amending the National Transportation Act and that there was room for improvement. In May 1984, my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), then Minister of Transport, was the first to suggest gradual deregulation of the transportation industry. At the time, our Government was thinking of a more flexible regulatory framework that would be better adapted to new economic configurations and the changing realities of the transportation sector.
We wanted a framework with less regulation that would enhance the development of Canada's transportation industry. At the same time, we wanted to ensure that guarantees would be provided for greater economic competitiveness.
Our policy not only had vision, it was firmly anchored in the realities of the day. Unlike the extremely bulky Bill we are considering today, my colleague, the former Minister of Transport, proposed a strategy for regulatory flexibility that could be defined as a step-by-step policy. At first, the strategy would basically deal with the air transportation sector and, in this respect, the Government at the time had provided a series of guarantees and specific conditions for deregulation in this sector.
However, by deciding to change everything at the same time, the present Government has raised a veritable wave of panic in many areas of the transportation industry, including air, trucking and railway transportation.
In fact, if we look at the alarming number of takeovers by large carriers of small airlines during the past two years, it is clear that the latter are very uneasy about this Bill.
In the trucking industry, for instance, people say there is a very real danger that the Canadian industry will be completely taken over by American interests. In the railway sector, CP Rail is afraid it will have to close down by 1992 if this Bill becomes law.
Although we endorse the principle of orderly deregulation, Mr. Speaker, our Party cannot accept the way this Bill has been brought forward nor the expediency of the legislative procedure chosen by the Government. We are strongly opposed to a series of measures contained in this Bill which, we believe, will be very harmful to the Canadian economy for years to come.
We also deplore the fact that this Bill does not contain the regulations required to establish, among other things, definite and credible safety standards for air passengers, as well as measures to guarantee adequate services for handicapped travelers and other provisions to protect jobs in the transport industry. There is nothing to assure us that deregulation will not entail widespread lay-offs, particularly in the air trasnsport sector. We oppose this Bill for its failure to offer guarantees to those who work in this major Canadian industry. Absolutely nothing tells us that our national transportation system will
continue to be-as it has been in the past and must indeed remain in future-the cornerstone of regional expansion in Canada.
What I am saying is more than my own personal conviction, more than the opinion of my colleagues of the Liberal Party of Canada who have examined this matter, for it reflects as well the views of a great many organizations, associations, and interest groups which have made it quite clear to the Government that this Bill has to be amended.
Regretfully I must say to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) that between June 26 last when the Bill-then C-126-was first tabled and November 4, 1986, when this Bill C-18 was introduced for first reading in this new session, the Government has turned a deaf ear to the quite legitimate representations made by a good many organizations representing thousands of Canadians-proof positive that this Government cares precious little about consultation as a democratic process. Worse still, the transport industry and Canadian consumers will bear the dire consequences of the Conservative Government's indifference or stubborness.
Mr. Speaker, the review of a blueprint act of such basic importance for the social and economic equilibrium of the country would have deserved a more balanced approach by the Government. It should have called for a great deal of caution in measuring the impact of such a de-regulation exercise, first, on passenger safety; second, on consumers, especially as concerns air fares; third, on jobs in the industry, as I mentioned earlier; fourth, on what is an acceptable level of foreign control; and finally, on regional development.
Unfortunately, the position of the Government seems to be set in concrete. Nothing has changed since publication of the paper "Freedom to Move".
You will recall that the Standing House of Commons Committee on Transport held public hearings throughout the country to collect the views of the public on the paper "Freedom to Move".
My colleague for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) is quite right to remind me that this Parliamentary Committee should normally have held hearings in all provinces and not only in major centers, but also in rural areas and the remote regions of our country since tranport in such a vast land as Canada has to meet the needs not only of urban dwellers, but perhaps even more so of people in remote areas.
However, the Committee held hearings only in four cities. In addition what I found was that the great majority if not all of those who made submissions to the committee or expressed their views about this initiative of the Conservative Government were opposed to it and to the Government's wish to deregulate transport in Canada so quickly and completely. The only witnesses we heard who supported the Government initiative were the shippers, the large shipping companies who see in this initiative a possibility of lowering the cost of moving their goods and products.
January 19, 1987

Of course, we recognize the need to develop a more effective and less costly transport service in Canada, but we maintain that this should not be done at the cost of other considerations and factors which are just as important. There must remain a fair balance in transport otherwise there will be very serious dangers and even the risk of a disaster in Canadian transport. I fear that some of the effects of implementing such a piece of legislation will not bring about lower transport prices as hoped by Canadian shippers but will probably mean higher rates for them in the middle- or long-term. What they want in the shortterm could in the long-term provide more disadvantages than advantages. Yet, this Government has refused to listen not only to the comments made before the Committee, but also to what was said when Bill C-126 was introduced. Indeed, at the Standing Transport Committee, the Conservative Members themselves expressed certain reservations about the Government initiative. Since they did not go far enough, the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party had to present minority reports to object to the majority report supported exclusively by Conservative Members of the Committee, even though many of these Members recognized several of the dangers inherent in the Government initiative. We would have expected at the very least that the Government would have taken into account the recommendations of its own Members, which it did not do in introducing Bill C-126.
I must say that Bill C-18 now under consideration is essentially a carbon copy of Bill C-126.
At a press conference, when the Minister of Transport was asked by a reporter what difference there was between the two Bills, the Minister did not know himself. He simply replied that there had been only a few technical changes. It is obvious that the Government has been deaf to the many representations made by the public and organizations opposed to its first Bill, for instance the Canadian Trucking Association.
The Canadian Trucking Association, following the presentation of Bills C-126 and C-127, wrote to the Minister indicating its opposition. In writing to me, the Executive Director had this to say concerning the Government:
Hopefully they will start over, but in their present form, these Bills are a disaster for the private sector common carrier transportation industry and truckers especially. In addition they have done nothing to even the playing field. U.S. truckers enjoy huge tax advantages and so forth. One would almost think that the future viability of the common carrier concept is no longer considered important in some respects.
That is the view of the Canadian Trucking Association about Bill C-126. As this legislation has been tabled again without amendment, the view of the Association will be the same.
Second, I have received a confidential representation from a federal public servant. He is very much concerned about the doing away of the air transport committee which has a responsibility to monitor the entrance and the exit of airlines.
National Transportation Act, 1986
He talks about the potential pitfalls of totally eliminating economic entry control in abolishing the test of public convenience and necessity, or the ignoring of certain elements of the test which has been carried out by the air transport committee, since May, 1984. This federal public servant has told me that he has been speaking not only on his own behalf but on behalf of a number of people who have spent their lives and careers working in this area.

Also, the opposition to the rail deregulation as it is contemplated by the Government has been very much opposed by the two railways, the CPR and the CNR. The following is CP Rail's position on Bill C-126:
If Bill C-126 were adopted in its present form, its plausible consequence as they relate to CP Rail are predictable.

system.
The Minister has totally ignored these representations. He also ignores the view of a senior official of the CNR who spoke on regulatory reform and railway viability at a conference in Vancouver last October. He was speaking about Bill C-126 which had not passed in previous sessions but was to be reintroduced in the new session. He said:
I am hopeful that when the Bill is reintroduced into the House, our legislators will carefully assess the long-term impact it could have on Canadian shippers.
Quite frankly, I believe that unless significant changes are made to the content of that Bill, we can expect results that will be unsettling to the transportation industry and, in the end, will not give shippers what they need.
That is the view of a senior vice-president of CN Rail and the Minister and the Government have totally ignored that point of view.

People are ignored not only in the transportation industry: even provincial Premiers are. Indeed, the Premier of New Brunswick, on behalf of the Council of Maritime Premiers, wrote to the Minister of Transport asking him to amend his legislation. He also wrote my colleague, the Hon. Member for Westmorland-Kent (Mr. Robichaud), in December 1986, saying how much he was concerned and disappointed with the attitude of the Canadian Minister of Transport, who had failed to amend Bill C-18 as suggested by the Atlantic Premiers in

the representations they made when Bill C-126 was originally introduced.
Once again, the Minister remained stone deaf to the representations asking for amendments to the Bill.
Union lobbying against transport deregulation is well known.
The Canadian Labour Congress held a press conference to indicate how much it opposed the kind of deregulation proposed by this Conservative Government, and to ask for amendments to the legislation if the Governement intended to proceed with the Bill, on the subject especially of job security for transportation workers.
Once more, the Minister remained totally unyielding on the representations that were made.
I am therefore forced to conclude, Mr. Speaker, that the Government has already cast its position in concrete, and that Mr. Keith Thompson, the official who has been acting on behalf of the Government since the beginning, who has met with all the parties concerned, who has had discussions with all those in the area of transportation who have a position to defend or interests to represent, has politely given the brush off to all those who met him and were told that the Bill is already drafted, and is not subject to change.
I would therefore like to tell the Minister it would be wiser to listen to the various parties involved in transportation who have amendments to suggest, rather than listen to Mr. Keith Thompson who apparently has decided the Bill was his baby and has to remain unchanged is spite of everything. Indeed Conservatives Members should remember that not so long ago they opposed the previous Government when we insisted on putting through the Bill amending the National Energy Program, and I would remind him of what a representative of a major Canadian association opposing the legislation was telling me recently. I would like to quote him, just to give the Minister food for thought:
"Keith Thompson will be to the transportation legislation what Ed Clark was to the national energy policy". I hope the Minister will reflect on this statement made by a representative of a national organization who is very much afraid that this official will play such a role that the Minister will have no chance at all to put his own imprimatur on the legislation.

speechtext: It's not. Let me reassure you.

speechtext:
So far there is no evidence to the contrary. When we begin studying this legislation in committee, we will know who is running the show. If the Minister is present, accepting or moving amendments, then we will know that he is the one who is carrying the ball on behalf of the Government. Until then, the impression will be that he is not running his own Department and that he does not know what the legislation he has submitted to the House is all about. I do hope that he will come forward with great interest and a sense of understanding for the various representations for amendments to this legislation.

It is with this in mind that we in the Liberal Party are preparing to discuss the Bill. As I said earlier, the principle of deregulation by itself, to promote stronger, more useful competition in transportation, is something that we certainly look forward to. We have no objection whatsoever to an orderly deregulation that would lead to greater competition in Canada's transportation industry. But our view is that, currently, the Government is totally insensitive to the representations that were made and we believe there are nefarious ramifications to that kind of roughshod deregulation as proposed by the Minister.
We thus want to be to a certain extent the spokespeople of all those Canadians whose views were not considered by the Minister when this Bill was drafted and we want to join them to denounce a legislation which we now feel to be inadequate.
We are specifically thinking of the safety area. We regret that the Bill does not contain any provision to prevent conditions which could effectively reduce air safety. The American experience teaches us that this is a real danger and that it is absolutely necessary to make sure that safety will not be jeopardized. The facts are as follows: In his report to the House of Commons for the fiscal year ended March 31 1985, the Auditor General, Kenneth Dye, stated that Transport Canada had been unable to check all carriers under its jurisdiction at least once a year. We cannot maintain that such safety standards are high and deregulation should in no way be introduced before strict and non-equivocal safety measures are implemented. The Liberal Party of Canada for sure will strongly object to any policy threatening the safety of airplane passengers in Canada.
In the United States, air travel is not as safe as before deregulation came into effect. The rate of fatal accidents and casualties has increased. Ronald Cape, President of the American company CETUS, states and I quote: "Commercial
January 19, 1987

flights are not as safe as before deregulation". And the President of Bache-Prudential, Mr. Harry Jacobs Jr. says: "To travel by plane is now much more dangerous." We merely want to make sure that what happened in the United States will not happen in Canada.
The tendency of this Tory Government to copy the Americans is really annoying. Why is it that every time something happens in the United States, a Conservative minister or Prime Minister always tries immediately to copy the Americans? I have nothing against the Government copying them when they do something good, but I certainly do not want us to copy what they have done in the United States in the area of air transport deregulation.
I have just mentioned that there is a major deficiency in the United States in the area of safety, an area that the Minister's bill has not provided for and that should be clearly stated with solid guarantees for air transport users in Canada. We know also that since deregulation was implemented, the number of employees in the air transport industry in the United States has greatly decreased.
And we are now witnessing a major concentration of American airlines. Due to deregulation, the concentration in the United States has been such recently that six airline companies now control as much as 80 per cent of the market in that country.
We have been quite concerned ever since the Government announced its desire to move forward with an urgent, quick and complete deregulation. A similar situation now exists in Canada: Since CP Air was bought by Pacific Western Airlines, two companies, Pacific Western Airlines and Air Canada, now control over 90 per cent of the Canadian market.
In my opinion, this is quite the opposite of what the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) himself said in the House when he introduced his Bill. On December 19, the Minister stated, and I quote:
The legislation that we are now presenting to the House has as its purpose the increase of competition in air-
It is the Minister of Transport himself, as reported in Hansard on page 2318, who said so. But the fact is that the Government has done nothing since the Minister announced its deregulation project to stop take-overs in the air transportation industry; not only has it done nothing to oppose these takeovers and prevent a greater concentration in Canada, but it has even encouraged it through remarks made recently in Parliament in reply to the question of an Opposition member.
Under the previous administration, before the Conservatives came to power, we had not only the two major national companies, Air Canada and CP Air, but also several important and profitable regional companies, like Pacific Western Airlines and Nordair which were doing very well, and others like Eastern Provincial, Quebecair, Air Ontario which were hanging on quite well to their shares of the market.
It is becoming obvious that deregulation is bringing a greater concentration in the air transportation industry, whereas the Government was saying, when it introduced the
National Transportation Act, 1986
Bill, that one the three basic principles of deregulation was increased competition among air carriers. What is happening is just the opposite. The Government will have to show us how all these take-overs will translate into increased competition.
Principles and rules of economics tell us that the greater the concentration, the less competition there is. It seems that the Government does not understand that since, as I said earlier, it did not chose to reject any of the nine take-overs which took place since it came to power.
In our opinion, this cannot continue. At the present time, Mr. Speaker, the transportation sector is in a state of chaos. I was talking a moment ago about uncertainty in the trucking industry, about the deep and understandable concerns of owners of trucking companies who feel they have been abandoned in an untenable situation.
Secondly, the two main railway companies in the country, CP Rail and CN Rail, are opposed to the Bill as proposed by the Minister while air transportation companies are changing ownership at a frantic rate.
It is clear that this Government has lost control of the situation in the transportation industry. Because of the Government's desire to deregulate too fast and too soon, this particular sector of our economy which has always been prosperous and provided steady and well-paid employment for thousands of workers across Canada, may be in for a very difficult time and fall prey to foreign interests.
What we cannot accept in this Bill is that it fails to put any restrictions on foreign control. Is this Government going to leave the sector wide open to anyone who wants to buy? In the United States, foreign control in the transportation industry is limited to 25 per cent. A foreign company cannot own more than 25 per cent of a transportation enterprise in the United States. Members of the Standing Committee on Transport and many intervenors who gave their comments on the Bill suggested this kind of restriction, but the Government, through its Minister, has never been willing to state, in no uncertain terms, that the transportation sector was one industry that had to remain Canadian. At no time did the Minister formally state that he would take steps to ensure that our major airlines and major trucking companies would remain in Canadian hands and that the transportation sector in general would remain in the hands of Canadian companies.
We are afraid that sudden deregulation will enable foreign interests, and especially U.S. interests, to take over the many trucking companies and airlines that would be unable to compete as a result of concentration of the industry among a few large companies, companies that will become far too powerful and thus be in a position to compete unfairly with the few small entrepreneurs that survive or try to survive in the transportation sector.
In concluding, I may say this Bill will need some thorough changes if it is to be at all useful to Canada's transportation sector. I hope that, in future, the Government will be more

January 19, 1987
National Transportation Act, 1986
receptive than it has been up to now to proposals for change with respect to this important legislation.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if and when passed, Bill C-18 is to be called a National Transportation Act. It is in the main a copy of the practices in the U.S. and results from their practices. I think the Bill should be known as a Bill to jeopardize safety in transportation. It should be known as an anti-service Bill. It should be known as an anticompetitive Bill. It should be known as an anti-sovereignty Bill.

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Make up your mind.

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
It should be known as an anti-regional economic development Bill, which is mentioned in the preamble to the legislation. This Bill enhances discrimination in transportation. We need a Bill which embodies good regulation, which is the real choice.
At the outset I would like to say that if, as, and when this Bill receives second reading, it must go to the Standing Committee on Transportat and hearings must be held all across Canada. The exercise carried out by the Government in its White Paper, Freedom to Move, was totally inadequate. It took a great deal of arguing, persuading and fighting by myself and my colleagues, the Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. Angus) and the Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) among others, to finally persuade the Government to allow the committee to travel. However, we were limited to three locations outside of Ottawa; we went to Vancouver, Winnipeg and Halifax. We missed seven provinces and both territories. As well, we left out the villages of Montreal and Toronto. That was a most inadequate opportunity for the people of Canada to present their views on a major government policy. That is why Canadians from all parts of the country must have the opportunity to express their views on this legislation.
The New Democratic Party is not arguing against up-dating the National Transportation Act. We believe that legislation of this magnitude must be up-dated from time to time. Twenty years have passed since the present Act was put in place. We believe that all regulations should be reviewed almost annually. Obsolete regulations should be gotten rid of, valid ones should be up-dated, and new ones to deal with new developments, practices and technology in transportation should be devised.
We also believe that the Canadian Transport Commission, or under any other name, should be streamlined to allow it to act more quickly and be more responsive. It must be more conscious of the needs of transportation consumers from the various regions of Canada as well as the needs of the transporters.
We believe that the Bill should not be dealt with until all the safety provisions and inspection facilities are in place and functioning. We know that the Government has proposed a railway safety board and that it is in the process of putting into place a national air safety board. We agree with that. However, it will take quite a while to get these boards established and functioning. We know that the Government has increased, to a certain degree, the number of inspectors. However, that is not nearly enough. Even without new legislation it would take many months, if not years, to obtain, train, and put in place the number of inspectors required. Once all of these items are in place and functioning we could consider an up-dated regime for national transportation legislation.
This legislation flies in the face of the very declaration of national transportation policy outlined in the Bill. The ramifications of this legislation and the eventual effects of it, if passed in its present form, will not provide a "safe, economic, efficient and adequate network of viable and effective transportation services" for most of the people and regions of Canada. The Bill ignores the economic imperative for the provision of equitable transportation services, rates, and fares for all of Canada. In fact, it will return this country to the situation of many decades ago; travellers, shippers and receivers will again be discriminated against because of where they happen to live, or where they happen to manufacture, grow, produce or process their products.
That inevitable discrimination will increase alienation felt by many Canadians in many parts of Canada. It will weaken our confederation and destroy our decades of effort for nationhood and co-operative federalism. It will further jeopardize our sovereignty and independence. I will have more to say about that later.
This legislation will provide access and advantage for United States railway and trucking companies in Canada which will not be available to Canadian railroads and trucking companies in the United States. That is a blatant betrayal of our independence. It is another example of the supine sell-out of our nationhood which is so evident in the free trade negotiations and the softwood lumber episode.
Earlier I mentioned discrimination in transportation against certain producers because of where they happen to be located. This Bill would have us make a 180 degree turn in what Canada has been trying to achieve for over 100 years. The Bill ignores Canadian history and, even worse, ignores the present Canadian reality. Historically transportation legislation and regulation have attempted, albeit not always successfully, to give each part of the country a reasonably equal opportunity to compete in far away domestic and foreign markets. It has attempted to require all Canadians to share in the cost of the various means of transporting goods right across our nation and to the rest of the world. Thus, it was no accident and no quirk of some contemporary political ideology that over the decades many transportation measures evolved within the framework of national transportation policy which were efforts
January 19, 1987

to achieve as large a degree of equity of treatment in the costs of transportation as was possible in our vast land.
I would like to remind the House of some efforts which have been made by this nation since the late 1800s. Recall the Crows Nest Pass Agreement of 1897, the statutory grain rates of the 1920s, and, presently, the Western Grain Transportation Act. As bad as it is, it is at least an effort to share in the costs of moving grain to export positions. There were the "at and east" rates, the Bridge rates, the Maritime Freight Assistance Act and the Atlantic Provinces Freight Assistance Act. There were special rates on settlers effects and on the products which settlers produced which were, in effect, in place and being used right up to the late 1950s. In addition, there was a system of agreed charges, which is still in place, which are negotiated among shippers, receivers and transporters. There have been many other arrangements which show the lengths that were gone to by this country to achieve a goal of reasonable equity of treatment in transportation.
This Bill ignores the Canadian reality. It fails miserably to take into account our geography, our sparse, widely-scattered population, our harsh climate and our sovereignty and independence. It returns us to the jungle of the so-called market forces, the myth that competition alone will provide for all of our country. The legislation would have us go back to the 18th and 19th centuries. It would leave us to the "invisible hand" of the market forces.
I would like to remind my Conservative friends that even the Conservatives in the early 1900s finally realized that that does not work. It particularly does not work in a nation as large as this, with our small population and our climate and geography. That has been shown through our experience historically and through the experience of many other countries over the last hundred years.
The legislation makes less effective and endangers the many programs now in place. We should be doing the opposite and strengthening those kinds of measures and devising new programs which take into account our nation and our economy as they are now. The legislation attempts to be an imitation, pale or otherwise, of American practices and incorporates much of its regime in the law and practices of transportation in Canada. The Government fails to realize that Canada is not the same as the United States of America, thank God. The Government fails to recognize that what we have in place now, as imperfect as it is with mistakes made in the past, is Canadian and meant for Canada. It suits Canada. It incorporates the fundamental principle of providing service as an equal if not greater priority to the obtaining of profit in transportation.
When I said the legislation is anti-competitive and antiregional and economic development, I did so partly because of who is the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) and where he comes from.

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
And where is he?
National Transportation Act, 1986

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
And where is he? If there is any Member of Parliament who should know about economic and regional disparity, about the requirements of different regions of Canada for extra provisions in the law and in the regulations which gives them at least some kind of equal treatment and opportunity to get into the markets of central Canada and the world, and in many cases the United States, it is the present Minister of Transport. But he is sponsoring legislation which flies in the face of real regional and economic expansion.
If we throw this wide open to the jungle of the so-called free market, free enterprise and competitive systems, the transporters will automatically-and one cannot blame them-gravitate to the largest and most lucrative markets. That means that the outlying regions, the isolated areas in the northern parts of Canada, will receive less service and less opportunity for economic development. If one had $100 million to invest in a new plant and was faced with discriminatory treatment in transportation costs if he located in Atlantic Canada, the Prairies, northern Ontario or northern Quebec, he would be crazy to build a plant in any of those places, no matter what temporary one-shot incentives might be offered by provincial and national Governments. One would be smart to build that plant next to or between Toronto and Montreal, somewhere in the so-called golden triangle.
The provision for confidential rates is not only anticompetitive, it flies in the face of what limited anti-competition law we have. It enhances the anti-competition in transportation. Let me illustrate how it does so. A railroad or consortium of trucking companies, or one major trucking company, can go to a large manufacturer or processor who moves 5,000 or 10,000 carloads a year and negotiate a confidential rate. Because it is confidential, the smaller manufacturer or processor not only cannot find out what the rate is but will not be able to get as good a rate because of the varying economies of scale, the size and volume of goods to be moved.
If I were a small farm implement manufacturer or food processor in the Prairie Provinces, I would be terrified of this legislation. Can you, Mr. Speaker, see either of the railroads or the larger trucking companies giving the same kind of rate to a small farm implement manufacturer in the Prairies who might ship 50 or 100 carloads a year as they would give to Massey-Ferguson, John Deere, J. I. Case or International Harvester Company who ship thousands of carloads a year? Anyone who believes they would is dreaming in technicolour. That is the kind of thing this legislation allows. It will discriminate against the development of manufacturing and processing capability in regions of Canada other than central Canada.
I mentioned earlier that this legislation is an attack on our sovereignty and independence. I would like to talk for a moment about the transborder implications of this legislation on transportation in Canada. The legislation will allow American railroads and trucking companies to do in Canada what Canadian railroads and trucking companies cannot do in the United States. The Bill is a fundamental reformulation of

January 19, 1987
National Transportation Act, 1986
the economic regulations of federal transportation undertakings. Of course the legislation would re-regulate the railroads intensively. It would place Canadian carriers at an unnecessary competitive disadvantage to American carriers in the competition for both transborder traffic and traffic which could be routed through the United States, although it originates or terminates in Canada.
I will illustrate the magnitude of the problem. Canadian Pacific alone earns $700 million annually from this type of traffic. If one adds to that figure the revenues earned by Canadian National and those earned by Canadian truckers one is looking at billions of dollar of traffic revenue.
The Canadian regulatory regime in respect of railways cannot be out of step with the American regime if Canadian railways are to compete effectively with their American counter-parts. This Bill contains a series of measures which would deny Canadian carriers the ability to compete on equal regulatory terms. Specifically, this Bill would enable American carriers to access traffic originating or terminating in Canada on terms and conditions which they are not required to grant to competitors in respect of their own traffic base. This Bill is an invitation for American incursions into the Canadian traffic base without fear that Canadian railways and truckers can retaliate in kind.
I am not known as one who has a great deal of love and affection for Canadian Pacific. I like to tell anti-CPR stories from the Prairies, and they are legion. However, it is still a Canadian company in which the Canadian taxpayers have invested billions of dollars since 1881. If we add to those billions of dollars private investment we will see that a Canadian railway company is jeopardized because of this blind following of Reaganomics, this myopic vision which Americans have that Canada is nothing more than the fifty-first state, an extension of the great U.S.A. Canada is much more than that. We in this Party will not hold still for the supine acquiescence which is contained in this legislation.

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: As if we are not having enough troubles with our friends south of the 49th parallel, not to mention our friends across the way, I could construct a list as long as my arm of the troubles we are having, including such matters as shakes and shingles, cattle, hogs, dressed beef and pork, softwood lumber, steel products, saltfish, groundfish, fresh fish, natural gas, and raspberries. It is about time to give not only the Government and this legislation the raspberry, it is time to give our friends to the south the raspberry as well. We must stand up for the right of Canada and Canadian transporters to have the same access in the United States as we provide the Americans in Canada, or else not provide that access.

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Unless and until that equity of access is made available to Canadian railroads and the Canadian trucking industry, then this legislation must not pass. That part of the legislation must be deleted.
I would now like to illustrate my point with respect to that access. Let us consider pulp products which originate in northern Ontario, northern Manitoba, Saskatchewan or even in British Columbia. At the present time these products travel via Canadian railways to Montreal. They then connect with Conrail to the northeastern United States and the American eastern seaboard. Under the provisions of this legislation American railroads can access that wood pulp for paper inside the Canadian border, take it back across the American border and haul it to the eastern seaboard, and all Conrail has to do is cancel the connecting rates it presently has between Montreal and the eastern seaboard of the United States. That is all Conrail has to do. The transportation of thousands of carloads a year of pulp would then be moved mainly on American transportation lines. An American railroad or trucking company can come into southern Ontario and obtain the products of manufacturing and processing plants destined for western Canada and the Pacific and take them down across the borders between Ontario and New York, Ohio, Windsor or the Sault and haul it by Conrail to Minneapolis and then on Burlington Northern to Seattle and Tacoma. That immediately places at risk traffic which would otherwise have gone through the Ports of Vancouver and Prince Rupert. My colleagues will have much more to say about that point as this debate continues.
On their way to Seattle and Tacoma cars carrying product manufactured and processed in Quebec or Ontario and destined for Manitoba can be taken off and brought up through Emerson and then to Manitoba. Cars destined for Saskatchewan can be taken off a train on the Burlington Northern and taken up to Portal. In the case of Alberta cars can be taken off Burlington Northern lines, run through Coutts and then into Alberta. The same situation applies to trucking.
Surely no self-respecting Canadian would hold still for that type of action. Surely no self-respecting Government would even contemplate such legislation which would jeopardize our sovereignty. Under this legislation, when, we feel that we are agrieved and require redress in our dealings with the United States in terms of transportation, we cannot go to a Canadian Government or a Canadian regulatory agency. What we will have to do is go on our hands and knees to the administration and regulatory bodies of the United States. It is demeaning and embarrassing. We will not stand quietly by and watch this Government, or any other Government, bring those types of provisions into transportation law in Canada.
In its blind efforts to copy and imitate the United States, no matter how inappropriate it is for Canada, the Government could take a good look at the U.S. experience. Probably there
January 19, 1987

is some validity to a massive deregulated regime in a country with a large, dense population and a lesser geography; then competition would work better, and there would not be discriminatory practices to isolated locations.
The United States has a smaller geography, 10 times the population, more than 10 times the volume of traffic, and a climate that is not nearly as harsh. The scale and volume of transportation movement provides it with the ability to move its goods at lower cost. The Government fails to recognize in this legislation that because of the nature of this country our costs in transportation will always be higher than those of the United States, Western Europe, or Australia. I suppose you could class the Scandinavian countries, the Soviet Union, and Northern Japan in a similar category as Canada. But the practices of the United States cannot be applied in Canada because of those differences.
The largest trucking company in Canada would rank about number 35 or 40 in the United States. We have a good trucking industry. There are some excellent Canadian companies operating and competing with rail, air, and marine, both here and in the United States. Under this legislation the incursions of large American trucking companies into Canada will do irreparable harm to the Canadian trucking industry.
In looking at the American experience and the hundreds of bankruptcies, mergers, acquisitions, and takeovers under its transportation regime, it has now reached the point where a handful of the major truckers directly and indirectly control some 75 or 80 per cent of truck traffic in the United States. So much for great competition.

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: That's Reaganomics.

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
In the airline industry the six major U.S. carriers that have evolved out of their regime since 1978 handle and control some 80 per cent of the traffic in the United States.
We have all seen the deregulation that has already taken place in the airline industry in Canada. There have been mergers, takeovers, and friendly agreements between a major carrier and small commuters and regional carriers, and the bankruptcies or near bankruptcies.
The matter of freedom of entry and exit in the trucking or airline industry means that a small or large reputable airline or trucking company that over the years has built up its routes, services, and customers, can be raided by a fly-by-nighter-if you will pardon the expression-in the airline or the trucking business that can move in at the peak of the market, cream the gravy off the top, and in the bad season pull out. That is not free enterprise. That is piracy.
What would happen to Bradley Air Services which operates an excellent air service into northern Canada when fly-by-nighters and two-bit charters move in on its efforts that serves communities as small as 300 people in the high Arctic? What would happen to its business? It would have no choice but to move its airline infrastructure and facilities out of the Arctic
National Transportation Act, 1986
and down into the Ottawa valley. That is the choice with which it would be faced.
Yet anybody who can con some banker into giving them a loan, lease two or three second-hand aircraft, hire some crews at less than half the pay because they have been laid off from some other airline, can get into business. If there was ever an appeal for a return to mediocrity it is this legislation.
The experience in the United States has not been all that great, but that is its business and its problem. Mark my words, because of the difference between that country and this one, the experience here will be magnified 10 times in terms of the impact, not only on our railways and trucking industry and airlines but on our ports and our shippers and receivers. The Government says that the intention of this Bill is to give them a better deal. The mythology that this will mean cheaper freight rates for everybody, cheaper airline service for everybody is just that, a myth.
Prices go down for a while in the big markets. Seat sales that apply to Toronto, Vancouver, Calgary, Edmonton, Halifax, and maybe Winnipeg, but leave out Moncton, Thunder Bay, and the Windsors of this world, mean that those people in those cities are discriminated against. The fares will be lowered and discounted, and we do not want to regulate that. If an airline, trucking company, or railway is dumb enough to charge less than what it costs, that is its problem. But all Canadians in every region should have the same opportunity for those types of benefits. They do not get them. That is another area where this Bill is discriminatory.
I wish to close by saying to the Government that the New Democratic Party wishes good regulation, because that is the real choice. The New Democratic Party wishes a viable, economic transportation industry in Canada that meets and serves the needs of the people in the regions of all of this nation, not just where the good, lucrative markets are.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I wish to move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. Angus):
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "That" and substituting the following therefor:
"Bill C-18, An Act Respecting National Transportation, be not now read a second time but that the Order for Second Reading be discharged, the Bill withdrawn and the subject-matter thereof be referred to the Standing Committee on Transport."

January 19, 1987

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 2 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, recent polls show that Canadians have a very low opinion of the Government. Apparently foreign countries share the same feeling.
Witness these results: the United States has a headlock on our softwood lumber sector, and its veto could spread to the management policies of other resource sectors. In a case of selective amnesia, the President forgets his commitments to combating the acid rain problem.
Meanwhile, eight French factory freezer trawlers are raping the fisheries stocks off Newfoundland's south coast. While Newfoundland's inshore fishermen suffer because of poor catches, the French vessels are catching over four times their proper quota. This blatant overfishing threatens the stocks and livelihood of many fishermen.
It is now high time for the Government to take action and bring this nonsense to a stop. Constructive internationalism has become a cruel joke to these fishermen.

Mr. Speaker, during World War II, Raoul Wallenberg, a Swedish diplomat, worked relentlessly to save the Jewish community of Budapest from extermination by the Nazis, by setting up houses to protect refugees under the Swedish flag, and negotiated tirelessly with Hungarian and Nazi authorities to save hundreds of Jewish lives.
Forty-two years ago, on January 17, 1945, Wallenberg, was last seen in the presence of Soviet armed forces. Although the Soviets claim that Wallenberg died of natural causes in 1947, a number of people have reported seeing him since. It has been suggested that he may still be alive. The Canadian Government has asked for an explanation from Soviet authorities, but the response given is unsatisfactory.
On December 9, 1985, Raoul Wallenberg became the first person to be named an honorary Canadian citizen. He has also been made an honorary citizen of Israel and, together with Winston Churchill, became the only other person to be awarded in his lifetime the title of honorary citizen of the United States.
It is only fitting that we remember this most distinguished citizen of Canada who risked his own life to save others. I call upon the Government to continue pressing Soviet authorities for a satisfactory answer to the whereabouts of Raoul Wallenberg and to secure his freedom.

Mr. Speaker, Margaret Laurence's death on January 5 should remind all Canadians how much we owe to our artists.
Through her characters, Margaret Laurence helped us to understand what it means to be Canadian, whether as an expatriate working in Africa, a single schoolteacher in a small prairie town, or an old woman coming to terms with death. Characters such as Hagar in The Stone Angel or Morag in The Diviners show Laurence's awareness both of the strength of women and of their vulnerability as humans.
They struggled to find purpose, integrity, and love, in a landscape and a society which were often harsh and unyielding. In her own struggle against the threat of nuclear war, Margaret Laurence took seriously her responsibility as a citizen of Canada and of the world.
Canada will survive as a nation to the extent that we keep our cultural sovereignty and adopt policies which allow writers like Margaret Laurence to flourish and to be widely read.

subtopic: FATAL ACCIDENT INVOLVING SWIFT CURRENT JUNIOR HOCKEY TEAM
FATAL ACCIDENT INVOLVING SWIFT CURRENT JUNIOR HOCKEY TEAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the afternoon of December 30, 1986, the Swift Current Bronco Junior Hockey Club left on a routine trip to Regina. Minutes later, the team bus slid on ice and overturned.
Killed were four outstanding young players: Trent Kresse, 20 of Kindersley, Saskatchewan; Chris Mantyka, 19 of Saskatoon, Saskatchewan; Brent Ruff, 16 of Warburg, Alberta; and home town favourite, Scott Kruger, 19.
As word of the tragic accident spread quickly across Canada and the world, the hockey fraternity everywhere reached out to Swift Current, a community left in shock and disbelief.
In the words of local writer, Brian Costello:
The four brave men who died should be remembered for the way there were, pleasant and special; just like their surviving team mates who struggle with courage to overcome the tragedy.
January 19, 1987

I am sure all Hon. Members will join with me in extending the sympathies of the House to the families and friends of these four young men.

subtopic: POTENTIAL FOR JOB CREATION-NEED FOR INVESTMENT
POTENTIAL FOR JOB CREATION-NEED FOR INVESTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as one of the top three industries in every region of Canada, the $22 billion tourism industry could become a real force for economic growth and job creation. An increase of just 1 per cent in tourism can generate about 8,000 jobs.
For tourism to reach its full potential, co-operation from the federal Government is needed to attract the investment dollars that will help to create world-class tourism facilities in Canada.
Since the growth of tourism in Canada depends on how Canada is promoted in foreign markets, the Government should discontinue its practice of hiring local people overseas, and put the delivery of its tourism program back into the hands of experienced and knowledgeable Canadian tourism experts. Measures such as these, as well as an increase in the federal tourism marketing budget, will go a long way toward helping the tourism industry to meet its goal of creating 600,000 new jobs by the year 2000.

maintopic: SOFTWOOD LUMBER EXPORT DUTY-EFFECT ON MARITIMES
SOFTWOOD LUMBER EXPORT DUTY-EFFECT ON MARITIMES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the decision of the Government to impose a 15 per cent export duty on Canadian softwood lumber has caused concern among wood producers in the Maritime provinces. Many producers feel their viability and the jobs they provide are in jeopardy.
Although five mills in New Brunswick were exempted from the duty, 125 mills are now hit with a provision that was installed to correct difficulties caused by extremely low stumpage rates in British Columbia, Alberta, Ontario and Quebec. This action could affect many mills, the jobs those mills provide, and the economic livelihood of many communities in a distressed region.
I urge the Government to undertake two initiatives. First, negotiate the entire Maritime region to an exempted status. Second, cause the effect of an increase to the stumpage rates in the four offending provinces, therefore removing the need for the 15 per cent export duty.
Some 22,000 jobs in the Maritimes are dependent upon a healthy and competitive lumber industry. We must ensure the policies we put in place affecting this sector will not result in job loss, greater unemployment, and continued regional disparity.

subtopic: AID SOUGHT FOR COMPLETION OF NEWFOUNDLAND ENCYCLOPEDIA
AID SOUGHT FOR COMPLETION OF NEWFOUNDLAND ENCYCLOPEDIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising to urge the Government to act quickly to help out Canada's only living Father of Confederation, Joey Smallwood. Mr. Smallwood, now in his eighties, is being financially hounded owing to his failure to complete his beloved project, a Newfoundland and Labrador encyclopaedia, because he is not well.
I would suggest that the Government pick up the cost of the completion of the valuable project started by Mr. Smallwood. This encyclopaedia is an invaluable resource not only for the people of Newfoundland and Labrador but for all Canadians and, as such, would be well worth the federal Government's investment.
It is a great travesty to see one of Canada's living legends being forced to deal with sheriffs at his advanced age and in his poor state of health. Surely the Government can find it in its heart to act now.

subtopic: CALL FOR WITHDRAWAL OF PATENT AMENDING LEGISLATION
CALL FOR WITHDRAWAL OF PATENT AMENDING LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amendments proposed in Bill C-22 by the Government amount to nothing more than a complete capitulation by the Government to the pressures of the American multinational drug manufacturers. The Canadian generic drug industry has been sacrificed on the altar of free trade negotiations, a victim of the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) insatiable need to surrender Canada's sovereignty to the United States.
I call upon the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) to withdraw this legislation immediately, which is an unjustified and unethical attack on the people of this country who have the misfortune to be ill. The sick or elderly should not be expected to pay the price for the Government's mistakes.
In 1983 Canadians saved approximately $200 million as a result of the Bill's amendment in 1969. What the Progressive Conservative Party wants to do is to change its name to the

January 19, 1987
Regressive Conservative Party because it wishes to go back to the pre-1969 days to give the multinationals a clear windfall profit.

subtopic: QUEBEC'S NEW FORESTRY POLICY-INITIATIVE TAKEN BY CERTAIN COMPANIES
QUEBEC'S NEW FORESTRY POLICY-INITIATIVE TAKEN BY CERTAIN COMPANIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, considering that Quebec's new forestry policy will be implemented as of next April 1, several pulp and paper companies in Quebec, particularly Domtar and CIP, have been carrying out excessive wood cutting operations for a number of weeks in the Abitibi-Temiscamingue region and in Quebec generally so as to produce more chips to show the Government of Quebec they are maintaining their five-year average wood cutting operations.
As a result of such excessive cutting these Quebec pulp and paper companies are endangering saw mills in Abitibi-Temiscamingue. Some 105,000 tons of wood chips worth $7 million are now piled up on the ground and more will be added in the coming weeks, enough to represent a value of $15 million.
Mr. Speaker, the Government of Quebec will have to look into this problem. There is room in Abitibi for two additional pulp and paper mills.

Mr. Speaker, after two years of Conservative administration I rise today in this House to highlight the positive aftermath of decisions made by our Government.
As a former businessman I vividly remember that, under a Liberal Government, I paid as much as 19 per cent on small business loans. The current rate is 10.75 per cent. I bought a house in 1983 and had to pay as much as 15 per cent in mortgage interests. Today I would be paying only 10 per cent. This is a major improvement, is it not?
Several economic indicators point to positive results throughout Canada. Consider the number of unemployed workers who have rejoined the labour market thanks to the dynamic and progressive policy of this Government. More than 600,000 jobs have been created in the past two years. One must be aware of and appreciate these facts which have made it possible for many of our fellow citizens to earn an honest living.
All these constructive measures taken by the Government will certainly not be headlined in the Star or the Enquirer, but such indeed is the new climate since our Government was elected. A number of improvements have been made and we can now see the beneficial results. You may rest assured that, in spite of all the obstacles it has to get over, our Government will continue to work towards better living conditions for all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, U.S. Senator George Mitchell is reported as saying:
We have, in all candor, been somewhat disappointed by the willingness of the Canadian Government to accept what I think are less than significant steps by the administration-I would hope that Canada's Prime Minister in the meeting this year will take a strong stand requesting meaningful action by the administration.
We have also learned that Senator Mitchell's frustration is widely shared by U.S. environmental groups that feel Canada let the administration off the hook by endorsing the envoys' report which contained no specific targets for acid rain reductions.
When will the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) wake up to the reality that acid rain cannot be tackled by way of a special relationship with President Reagan? When will the Prime Minister realize that the envoys' report has not reduced acid in Canada by one ounce? The Government has wasted two years. The cost of this inaction is staggering. It is high time the Prime Minister dealt with the substance of the issue and not just with smoke and mirrors.

maintopic: TAX ON SOFTWOOD LUMBER MANUFACTURED PRODUCTS
TAX ON SOFTWOOD LUMBER MANUFACTURED PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Government is protecting Americans from their own softwood lumber. Not only has it levied a 15 per cent tax on softwood exports to the U.S. but the Government has also put this tax on Canadian products made from American softwood.
A manufacturer in my riding imports American lumber and sells his finished products back in the United States. However, the Conservative Government charges him 15 per cent when the American softwood goes back over the border. That is not all. The Government is not charging 15 per cent of the sawmill price but is putting the tax on the full price of the finished
January 19, 1987

product. Even if the manufacturer buys lumber that is exempt from the export tax from a Canadian mill, he has to pay 15 per cent on any finished goods produced by Canadian workers. This ensures that our manufacturers cannot compete and that Canadian jobs will be lost. Conservatives are exporting jobs to the United States and are ensuring that Canadians remain simple hewers of wood.

maintopic: EFFECT OF SOFTWOOD LUMBER EXPORT DUTY
EFFECT OF SOFTWOOD LUMBER EXPORT DUTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1983 our nation was faced with the threat of a countervailing duty against softwood lumber. We then had 19 per cent of the market and we won that decision.
In 1986 we were confronted with another CVD petition. The Canadian dollar value was lower and American protectionist sentiment stronger. Our share of the U.S. market had grown to well over 30 per cent. Last October we lost that decision and a 15 per cent CVD was imposed.
Now it is January, 1987. Through negotiations, the duty has been removed. Canadian lumber producers no longer have to post bonds at the border. Over $600 million in reforestation funds will pour into provincial coffers. We British Columbians know that we have not been replanting all that we cut. Now we will.
What a fascinating debate we will have on this issue in the House. The NDP will be fighting for the corporate forest interests and the Ontario Premier, while the Tories will be defending the position of the forest unions, the IWA, and the B.C. NDP. We do live in interesting times.

Mr. Speaker, on January 22 Ukrainian-Canadian communities will be raising the Ukrainian flag across the country commemorating Ukrainian Independence Day. The emergence of Ukraine as a free state, though for a brief time only, symbolizes the spirit of freedom which continues to live in the hearts of the 35 million Ukrainians now living under Soviet oppression. Although it is the largest nonRussian, eastern European state, Ukraine is denied the freedom of determining its own fate.
In 1975 a 35-nation conference signed an accord in Helsinki which linked human rights, culture, and education with security and co-operation, which includes the right of self-
Oral Questions
determination. Over one-half of Soviet Russia is made up of non-Russian nations. Those nations will ultimately have the right to define their destiny and shape their own identity. World pressure should make it so.

subtopic: ALGOMA ARTISTS' DESIGN SELECTED FOR DOLLAR COIN
ALGOMA ARTISTS' DESIGN SELECTED FOR DOLLAR COIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government's incompetence usually draws strong criticism and such was the case when it lost the master dies for the new Canadian dollar coin a few weeks ago. However, it is an ill wind that does not blow good for someone. The loss of the original dies has resulted in the selection of the loon design, the work of Robert Carmichael, an artist from Sylvan Valley near Echo Bay in Algoma district, which is in my constituency.
Mr. Carmichael, who was born in Sault Ste. Marie, is a graduate of Carleton University and of the Ontario College of Art. He is an outstanding artist who often paints landscapes of northern scenes. The loon design reminds us of our rich Canadian heritage of northern lakes and waterways, which are the loon's natural habitat. This design will be used on some $450 million worth of Canadian coins and will bring historic renown to one of Algoma's most talented artists.

Mr. Speaker, I think the question was as to whether I had knowledge of that. If that was the question, the answer is no.
