speakeroldname: Hon. Pat Carney (Minister for International Trade):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you are aware that we have finally reached an agreement with the United States on the issue of softwood lumber, after months of intense effort on behalf of the Government, and after a study of the many complex issues that this matter brought before us.
I wish to remind you that one of the reasons why this is so important, and the measures we are taking are so vital, is that Canada is very much a forest nation. Including our northern territories, all of Canada in some way is involved with forestry, as is all of Canada involved in some way with trade.
I wish to assure the House that in bringing forward this measure we have acted in the national interest, we have acted consistent with our GATT obligations, and we have acted in a way that is infinitely better than the alternative before us, which was to accept a countervailing duty.
In terms of the national interest, I would like to review with you that we in our agreement moved to protect our sovereignty. The Opposition would allow the U.S. to overrun our forests. We acted to protect our revenues. The Opposition would pay these revenues to the U.S. We acted to protect our industries. The Opposition would expose those industries to other countervails. We acted to protect jobs. The Opposition's preferred option, countervail, would cost jobs.
In terms of dealing with our GATT obligations, I would like to remind the House that Canada is an international trader. We are in the big leagues in trade. Canada, along with the European Community, the U.S., and Japan, are the four big trading interests which account for 40 per cent of the world trade. The Opposition would take us out of the big leagues. The Liberals would send us down to the minors. The NDP would leave us on the bench.

January 19, 1987
Softwood Lumber Products Export Charge Act
In terms of the countervail, I can only quote the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). As the Prime Minister has stated, in terms of the countervail if we had a choice between this agreement and perfection, we would have taken perfection. But we had a choice between this negotiated agreement on our terms, and a countervail. In this agreement we have the best settlement possible, given the alternatives which we faced.
I would like to briefly outline the options, the process, the demands, and the results achieved in this agreement. First, I wish to remind the House that this is not a new issue. Our research shows that the earliest attempts to block softwood lumber exports to the U.S. were in 1892.
In 1983, faced with a similar countervail threat, we won the preliminary determination. However, in 1986 we lost the preliminary determination, and a 15 per cent duty was declared. Therefore, under international law, and under U.S. trade law, we faced three options. We could fight and risk losing the case and paying countervail duties to the U.S. Treasury. We could plead guilty that our stumpage programs were subsidies. This is a position that Canada has always maintained is not the case. Our second option was to plead guilty that our stumpage programs were subsidies and enter into a suspension agreement to keep the additional moneys in Canada. The third option open to us was to negotiate a settlement in order to protect the thousands of Canadians who work in the industry, while protecting the right of the provinces to manage their resources, and to keep forest revenues in Canada.
The Canadian Government engaged in full consultations with the provinces, labour, and industry. We explored all the options consistent with our duty to protect Canada's interest.
A split developed between the provinces as to what approach we should take. This is important, because this Government has always maintained the constitutional right of the provinces to their natural resources, a right that the Liberal Government has ignored in the past.
Ontario wished to proceed to the final decision in the hopes of reversing it, or if that failed, challenging it in the U.S. courts. British Columbia and Quebec are the major owners with 80 per cent of the forests. They favoured negotiating a suspension agreement to keep the money in Canada.
In discussion with the U.S. Commerce officials we became increasingly convinced that notwithstanding our strong case, we would lose the final determination. Such a final determination would have been an open invitation for any special interest group in the U.S. to file a petition against our other resource exports, because that would have put on the books, through the final determination, a precedent which could be used against our other export industries. Thus, in November, I concluded that fighting the case through to the finish would almost certainly entrench a dangerous legal precedent, and see the resulting countervail duties flow to the U.S. Treasury. I may remind the opposition Parties that the duties could well have been higher than 15 per cent. The U.S. industry was asking for
36 per cent. We had no reason to believe that it would be safe to assume that we would only have a 15 per cent duty.
It is our position that we do not fight to lose cases. We fight to win cases. On the other hand, the suspension agreement approach which was favoured by B.C. and Quebec was equally unpalatable. That would have surrendered our forest management policies to the U.S. Government. That was totally unacceptable to the Government of Canada.
The proposal that I developed with Secretary Baldrige came the closest to meeting the objectives of all parties. It was presented to the First Ministers' Conference in November. The Premiers agreed to see if we could explore it. The benefits of seeking a negotiated settlement were very clear. It would meet both national and provincial objectives, increased revenues would be kept in Canada, and these could be used to replenish the forests. These revenues will be returned to the provinces and the provinces have the right to use them for silvaculture, reforestation, worker retraining, or other things within their constitutional jurisdiction.
The provinces would retain their flexibility in determining stumpage pricing, which is very important to the two provinces that had stumpage increases in their systems planned and were caught in the vice of the threatened countervail.
It would avoid the dangerous development in U.S. countervail policy by having the petition withdrawn, because it was central to this negotiation that in return for a negotiated settlement the actual petition that was brought by the U.S. intra groups, the U.S. coalition of lumber, would be withdrawn, and further conflict between the provinces on how they determine their natural resource management policies would remain unimpaired. Unlike a suspension agreement, the U.S. authorities could not infringe Canadian sovereignty by policing provincial management practices.
The agreement we reached with the United States meets all of these objectives. It is important to stress that it is supported by the nine provinces that own the resource, the union that represents the forestry workers, and important elements of the industry. For our B.C. Members of Parliament, it may be useful to note that the B.C. NDP critic, Bob Williams, was reported in the media as saying that the softwood accord was "a pretty good deal". It was the best that could be obtained in difficult circumstances. Moreover, it was reached on our terms, because the key clauses that were on the table at the start of the negotiations were on the table at the end of the negotiations.
Much has been made by the critics about the alleged infringement of Canadian sovereignty. This is really a phoney issue. All countries regularly conclude international agreements in which they agree to restrict their freedom of action, even in the Auto Pact that the NDP is so worried about.
All agreements between countries is an exercise of sovereignty, by the very willingness and ability of countries to enter
January 19, 1987

into them. Our sovereignty is undiminished and, if at some future date we were to decide to terminate the agreement, that too would be an exercise of sovereignty.
What has Canada agreed to do in this agreement? During the course of the negotiations the U.S. coalition made many demands upon Canada. It is fundamental to understand that under existing U.S. trade law any interest group in the United States can bring this kind of action against any Canadian export. This is why we are seeking to negotiate a new trade treaty with the U.S.-to change these rules so that we avoid these kinds of border disputes.
One of the demands which the U.S. coalition sought was to establish a floor price regardless of market conditions. It sought to dictate how Canadian stumpage policies would operate. It demanded specific changes in provincial systems within a defined time frame, with a joint supervisory committee to oversee the changes.
The opposition Parties forget that what the U.S. coalition was asking for was a $ 1.1 billion increase in stumpage in one year. That is what they were seeking, and that is what they did not get. That is almost three times the existing levels of stumpage collected in the country.
If the idea of the joint board had been accepted, the U.S. Government would be able to dictate how our policies should be made and implemented. That was totally unacceptable to Canada, and we rejected it out of hand.
The U.S. administration has expressly recognized Canadian sovereignty in its statement of January 2, wherein it said that "The United States Government will not be concerned with how Canadian authorities make changes in their forest management practices. When they do so or what form these changes take. These are matters for Canadians to decide."
I also assure the Opposition that I personally telephoned Mr. Yeutter, the U.S. trade representative, to make it clear, in terms of the letter which was quoted, that the U.S. had a choice-either we had an agreement on the terms that the U.S. accepted with the statement I have just read from Ambassador Niles, or the U.S. would be in contradiction of the agreement it had just signed. These are all the essential qualities-
What did he say?

The Opposition asks: "What did he say?" They issued the statement; that is what they did. They issued the statement which said: "These are matters for Canadians to decide".
The Hon. Member has been spreading misleading information about this matter in a way which is detrimental to the national interest.
Hear, hear!

The only item which is the subject of consultation and agreement is the calculation of the value of any
Softwood Lumber Products Export Charge Act
changes in the export tax, because the export tax is a 15 per cent tax at the border. At some point in time it is planned to phase it, in whole or in part, into increased stumpage, if that is what the provinces wish to do, and the U.S. has the reasonable right to ensure that the conversion from an export tax to stumpage meets the criterion of 15 per cent.
It must not be forgotten that if the countervail had been imposed, Commerce officials would have been coming into Canada, as they did on the preliminary determination, and would have verified provincial and industry books. They would be in the forest services records, they would be in the forests, and they would decide unilaterally how we were going about this method. That unacceptable practice has been avoided.
Under the agreement the information we will provide to the U.S. is essentially in the public domain and does not involve U.S. officials entering Canada to audit and verify it. Reaching this agreement is a major accomplishment. When compared with a suspension agreement, the settlement is infinitely preferable. Like a suspension agreement the money stays in Canada but, more important, the intrusive policing of provincial management practices which a suspension agreement entails has been avoided.
What the Opposition also fails to realize is that if the countervail had gone into effect as expected-and I hope every B.C. Member is conscious of this-the Canadian forest industry would have been faced with a double whammy of both a duty and an increase in stumpage, because the only way one can get rid of a countervail is to increase stumpage to the point where the Commerce Department in the U.S. unilaterally decides that the alleged subsidy was offset.
Here we have an industry which now has a 15 per cent tax that with a countervail would have had both the tax and increases in stumpage to offset it-a 30 per cent plus double whammy. We knew that the Canadian forestry industry could not sustain it. We negotiated the settlement because we knew the double hit of 30 per cent plus would break the industry.
In this we were supported by the IWA which said that the negotiated settlement was absolutely essential. I would like to read the particular paragraph where the IWA said: "We would suggest that many negative comments have been both ill-informed and ill-founded". The IWA also told us: "We . . . strongly believe that it was absolutely essential to conclude a negotiated settlement with the United States which will guarantee that the increased taxes on softwood lumber shipments to the United States be kept in Canada".
I am really looking forward to British Columbia NDP Members of Parliament returning to their ridings, because the IWA has stood by this even when the NDP asked them to back off. The NDP asked them to back off, and the IWA would not. The IWA has been barnstorming around, saying: "This is the letter which we sent the Minister and this is the letter we stand by".

Hear, hear!

January 19, 1987
Softwood Lumber Products Export Charge Act

Some critics have predicted massive job losses resulting from our agreement.
As a federal Minister of course I am always concerned about the employment effects of government actions, but we must recognize a few points. First, the forest industry has always been a cyclical one with ups and downs. Second, as the shakes and shingles tariff has shown, the effects of a tariff or charge are difficult to predict. The NDP were maintaining that thousands of people would be laid off and that terror would reign in the woods. As a matter of record, that industry, although it has suffered, has in no way experienced nearly the catastrophe which the NDP suggested.
I can also say that the IWA has made the following clear, in terms of job loss in its letter to me:
The second assumption is that the Canadian sawmilling industry will be unable to compete under the burden of a 15 per cent export levy. We regret the fact that not all Canadian sawmills will survive, and that some jobs will be lost.
As of course does the Government. It continues:
It should not be assumed, however, that a substantial portion of the Canadian sawmilling industry will disappear.
In its letter it gives some well reasoned arguments why.
Where do we go from here? Last week I, along with my colleague, the very able Minister of State for Forestry and Mines (Mr. Merrithew), met with the provincial Ministers. We reviewed the agreement. A federal-provincial task force has been established to review all aspects relating to the implementation of the agreement. We will have a subgroup of forest Ministers, headed by the Hon. Len Simms of Newfoundland, which will study the matter of replacement measures. We will work together to ensure that we iron out the problems which the industry faces.
Before closing, I want to deal with some side issues which have been raised today in debate or in the newspapers. First, one of our colleagues from New Brunswick is worried about the impact on his province. I want to point out that the Government of Canada maintained for his province the 92 per cent exemption on lumber exports contained in the preliminary. In the preliminary decision, 20 firms won an exemption, and 92 per cent of New Brunswick's exports were thus protected. In the negotiations and in the final determination mechanism, the U.S. was moving to take away those exemptions and to expose the New Brunswick industry. We fought for New Brunswick and we maintained the exemption.
In the so-called Dennison letter, which is a self-serving letter, the U.S. told lumber producers, in effect, all the things they could not win at the bargaining table. It is a side letter which has no standing in Canada. It is a side letter which the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) is trotting around as some sort of legal document. He knows that the negotiator for the U.S. side told him that it was a letter for Americans, that it had no standing. He was told that personally by the U.S. negotiator in Washington last week. Knowing
that, and having been told that it has no standing for Canadians, he still purports that this is some kind of legal document, and that is misleading the public.
Shame, shame!
The NDP today in, I hope, an innocent error suggested that the export tax would apply to the added value of manufactured products. That is not true. We negotiated very hard.
I checked half an hour ago.
The Hon. Member said he checked. He did not check with us.
A half an hour ago.
He did not check with the Government of Canada because we negotiated an arrangement where the tax applies only to the lumber inputs, not to the added value.
Phone your people in London, Ontario.

I refer the Hon. Member to the agreement. That was the second last clause that we dealt with. This too is better than a countervail because a countervail would have been applied to the whole product, as the New Democratic Party was suggesting.
In terms of jobs, I want to point out that the Members of the NDP travelled around this country with a task force and, as the media reported, they could not Find any lay-offs directly attributable to the export tax, which is quite proper. I am glad that the Minister, although she has claimed on several occasions that this was a great victory for Canada, did not go one step farther and claim it was historic. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that it will go down in history as the greatest sell-out in the history of our negotiations with the United States and the greatest betrayal of a major industry of Canada by a Minister who should be responsible for export potential.
Our industry, with very few exceptions, will pay a 15 per cent export tax on every bit of softwood lumber going into the United States. It will cost the lumber industry on the basis of this tax about $600 million, maybe more. As I will attempt to portray to the Elouse, as this tax is converted into a timbercutting fee or a stumpage fee at the provincial level, it may well amount to a tax of $950 million to $1 billion against the industry, not just for one year but year after year. Mills will close. Thousands of Canadian workers will lose their jobs and all the Minister has to say to this House, and said earlier, is that "by limiting the Americans only to the arithmetic we kept them out of our forests, out of our books and out of our hair." She made that argument in an interview with a reporter from The Globe and Mail on January 6. She repeated it here today. I want to tell the Minister and the Government,-the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has just left-that this country surrendered more sovereignty than I can remember in any individual transaction.
The United States now has the right to set the price of our exports of lumber, to set the tax against it, to review how that tax is converted into a fee and to reach into all the documentation necessary to buttress that position. It was a complete sellout.

That is why our forestry industry was so confident it would be able to repeat its success before the U.S. courts in 1983, since neither the facts nor the legislation have changed. At this point I wish to deal with the central matter as I see it of this Government's failure to defend a crucial principle in negotiations which have been going on, as the Minister herself pointed out, for a number of years, not simply for a number of months. When it comes to stumpage the reality is that the Government of Canada, with the support of all Parties of the House and with the support of the industry, won its case before the U.S. tribunals at that time. The central part of the 1983 decision was that stumpage fees-that is to say a provincial royalty on our forest products-would not in principle be deemed to be a subsidy. That was a fundamental part of our argument at the time, and a fundamental part of the reason for the acceptance of our argument in 1983. It ought to have remained a fundamental concern of the Government in accepting the notion of sovereignty that neither the United States nor any other country ought to have the right to tell Canadian provinces what they are to sell their resources for. That ought to have remained at the centre of contention, but it did not.
An article in the most recent issue of The Financial Post, and I am sure the Secretary of State for External Affairs reads that paper regularly, points out that if the Government had hung tough with its case it could well have won the decision just as we on this side of the House and many others, have been saying. But it did not do so.
Among other points that are emphasized in the article to which I refer is the information that the International Trade Commission had presented to it in December a report by its own staff which showed that the claims by the U.S. industry with respect to having been so badly injured by Canadian exports in softwood had been greatly exaggerated. In terms of the International Trade Commission's final decision, which would have been rendered in February had the Government not negotiated this particular settlement, that was very important. I say that because in terms of the International Trade Commission's final decision it not only had to make a decision about what was or was not a subsidy but it also had to deal with the question of injury. Clearly, the importance of this information is that the International Trade Commission itself had documentary evidence that the case for injury had been greatly exaggerated by U.S. industry.
On behalf of my colleagues, and much more important than that given the importance of this decision, on behalf of the Canadian softwood industry, the workers and companies in it, as well as all our other resource industries which can now be affected by this decision, the Government of Canada ought to have hung tough with its original case. Up until September, 1986 both the present Minister and her predecessor made a series of statements about the great confidence that they had in our traditional Canadian argument that stumpage fees were not in any sense a subsidy. They repeated that argument. They had the support of all Parties in the House. They had the support of the industry, and of the provinces. The Minister says that is true. Then something happened. Mr. Vander Zalm was elected in the Province of British Columbia.
Shortly after charmingly appearing together with the Minister in her householder to her constituents, the same Premier started to talk publicly about renegotiating stumpage levels on the one hand and about the importance of the Government of Canada beginning a negotiating process instead of waiting for the quasi-judicial tribunals to make a decision. It was at that time that the Minister made her first statement, the first of many final offers, I say to the Minister. We heard that immortal phrase in September when she offered the 10 per cent settlement. The 15 per cent final settlement came later. The 10 per cent came, then we have what the Minister correctly alludes to as the next phase, the preliminary ruling on October 16. That was a little shocking to the Minister. I do not like doing this at great length, but I wish to put this on the record because it is amusing. If it were not so sad, it would be really funny. The Minister stated after this ruling that we "will fight this all the way... Today it's lumber. Tomorrow it could be any number of issues".
The Minister further stated:
We all agreed that this ruling is deplorable, artificial and contrived, and does not stand up to extensive analysis.
The Minister also stated that it "strikes directly at the sovereign right of a government to manage its own natural resources".
The Minister then stated that, "we will fight to reverse this verdict". That great historical battle that the Minister waged lasted a few days. What the Minister said was absolutely true. That was not enough because on October 27, 1986 the Minister stated the following. This is rather important, and I hope that she remembers it:
This decision has concerned us and should concern all of the United States' trading partners, because we view it as an unacceptable attempt to impose U.S. views on how other governments should manage their natural resources. Furthermore, we feel that this preliminary ruling by the U.S. Commerce Department has no basis in U.S. law, is badly flawed, and is inconsistent with the U.S. obligations under the GATT.
The Minister was right then. We are right now in reaffirming the same point. The Minister ought to have stood by her argument and she might have won.

The Government of Canada will take no action, and will take all reasonable steps to ensure that no other governmental body in Canada takes any action, directly or indirectly, which has the effect of offsetting or reducing the export charge or replacement measures, except as provided in this Understanding.

This is spelled out in the related letter sent out by the U.S. officials. For example, this wording clearly prohibits action by the Government related to the Employment Support Act to support employment in the lumber industry. In 1971, for example, this specific Act was used to make no fewer than 769 grants totalling over $10 million in support of almost 22,000 jobs that were then put at risk because of a U.S. surtax.
The point I wish to make is that we had the right to use that legislation in Canada at that time to protect workers who were injured. Because of the agreement that this Government has entered into, our sovereign power as a nation is restricted, and we can no longer take that type of action to protect our workers.

PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   RIGHT HONOURABLE LESTER B. PEARSON STATUE TO HONOUR HIS MEMORY
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of honouring the memory of the Right Honourable Lester B. Pearson by commissioning a statue of him to be placed on Parliament Hill.
He said: As you know, Mr. Speaker, on October 2, 1986 I issued a press release to suggest to the Canadian people that right here on Parliament Hill we should have a statue to honour the late Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson.
First I should like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Scarborough Centre (Mrs. Browes) who introduced a similar resolution last year, word for word except that the name was different. At the time the Hon. Member for Scarborough Centre proposed that a statue be displayed to honour the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker. As Hon. Members will recall the House unanimously adopted the motion on the very day it was introduced and debated. Mr. Speaker, I dare hope, therefore, that for the same reason, Hon. Members from all sides of the House will support this motion today and adopt this initiative for the purpose of setting up a statue in honour of a really great Canadian, a tremendous statesman, a former leader of my Party, a man who is no longer with us and who has served his country so well, the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson.
Mr. Speaker, one of the most distinguished prime ministers in the history of this country was born 90 years ago. Lester B. Pearson was a prominent diplomat, a prestigious figure who greatly contributed in placing our country at the forefront at the international scene. It was therefore quite fitting that the building which the Department of External Affairs uses as its headquaters should bear its name.
Lester Pearson has indeed left tangible marks in the direction of Canadian foreign policy. As a tough politician, he had undertaken the reconstruction of the Liberal Party of Canada and had fought to maintain Canadian unity.
Following studies in history which led to a teaching career, Lester B. Pearson decided to join the Department of External Affairs which was made up at the time of a handful of officers. Having attracted attention very early because of his insight and his talents as an observer on the international scene, Mr. Pearson was sent to London in 1935 as First Secretary of the Canadian High Commission. This assignment made it possible for him to follow very closely the escalation which led to the outbreak of hostilities in Europe. Deeply influenced by these events, Mr. Pearson became convinced of the need to develop a collective defence.
Shortly after his return to Canada in 1941, Mr. Pearson was posted in Washington where, through his charm and courtesy, he became one of the most admired foreign personalities. In 1945, he was appointed Canadian Ambassador to the United States and, the same year, he took part in the San Francisco Conference which led to the creation of the United Nations.
In September, 1946, Mr. Pearson was summoned to Ottawa by then-Prime Minister Mackenzie King who offered him the position of Deputy Minister of External Affairs. In spite of the assignments related to his position, he continued to follow closely the activities of the United Nations.
Moreover, the development of closer relationships between Canada and its main allies, the United States and Great Britain, was also one of his main concerns. He showed his great talents as an ingenious intermediary when Canada joined NATO.
Our Prime Minister of the time, Mr. Pearson, was a great Canadian for his diplomatic initiatives. He proposed a United Nations peace force to evacuate French forces from Egypt. This realization earned him the Nobel Peace Prize the following year. He is the only Canadian Prime Minister ever to be a recipient of the Nobel Peace Prize.
This stand he took was, however, to create much antagonism domestically. Many criticized the Government's position as failing to support Canada's ally, Britain. When the Liberals were defeated in 1956 and Mr. St. Laurent stepped down as leader, Mr. Pearson won the leadership convention and began the rebuilding of our great Party. It was no easy task. With such brilliant people as Walter Gordon, Mitchell Sharp,
January 19, 1987

Maurice Lamontagne and Paul Martin, we re-established the presence of the Liberal Party on the national scene which made possible the 1963 electoral victory.
In a period characterized by intense turmoil and redefinition of the country's aspirations, the Pearson Government accomplished many important reforms. It left behind an impressive body of legislation, most notably the Canada Pension Plan, the universal medicare system, the unification of the Armed Forces and a revised Transportation Act. As well, it initiated a new approach to the problem of Canada's disadvantaged regions through the Department of Regional Economic Expansion.
The motion I am requesting today asks for the erection of a statue to Lester B. Pearson. I believe this motion is very timely and appropriate. Mike Pearson was one of the greatest Prime Ministers this country has had. Moreover, his renown abroad was perhaps greater than that of any other Prime Minister. In this regard, a tribute to his memory on this the 90th anniversary of his birth will certainly be appreciated by his family and friends as well as being an honour for all our fellow Canadians who, partisanship aside, undoubtedly recognize that Lester B. Pearson did place a very distinct imprint upon Canadian society.

Mr. Speaker, I have already contacted the representatives of the National Capital Commission to seek their advice on this issue and I am happy to report that through its president, Mrs. Jean Piggott, the National Capital Commission has indicated its support for this initiative and has offered to co-operate in the search for a proper location to set up this statue.

It is interesting to note that presently there are statues for every Prime Minister who has been elected except one, that of Lester Pearson. There are no statues of Prime Ministers in the late 1800s who came in a succession, but none of them were elected. There is another Prime Minister for whom a statue was built, but it was later decided not to erect it on Parliament Hill because members of the family perhaps did not feel it appropriate, or they did not like the statue.
I ask for the consent and the support of this House for this non-partisan and most appropriate measure to honour one of Canada's greater citizens, Lester B. Pearson.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   RIGHT HONOURABLE LESTER B. PEARSON STATUE TO HONOUR HIS MEMORY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure that I join in the debate on the motion proposed by the Hon. Member for Glengarry- Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria). I gather the motion has been precipitated by recent events, namely, the erection of the statue of the Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker, which was a very successful venture. As a result of the unanimous disposition of this House at the unveiling and ceremony commemorative to Mr. Diefenbaker the event was a total success. We had a magnificent day. There was general acclaim, not only in
Parliament Hill
Ottawa but across the country. For that very reason I gather that my hon. friend has discovered that these kinds of initiatives can be applauded by all Members of the House. Indeed, we are prepared to give favourable consideration to a motion of this nature.
I might observe, Sir, that a statue of this nature has not been erected within the precincts of Parliament for some 11 years. Since there was a commemorative statue erected to honour Sir Wilfred Laurier some 59 years ago only four statues have been constructed within the boundaries of Parliament, those of Prime Ministers Borden, King, St. Laurent and Diefenbaker.
I think I indicated in my remarks at the ceremonies acknowledging Mr. Diefenbaker that this was the kind of tribute and collective action that should be taken by Members here and now who, while they enter into dispute from time to time, do recognize contributions made. It is appropriate and fitting that we recognize the contribution of Members, no matter from which Party they come or which opinion they express from time to time. It is appropriate that we specifically recognize and honour those who have served as Prime Minister no matter from which Party they come.
I have suggested to the Department of Public Works that it carry out a study to determine, from an historic point of view and with a view to giving us guidance for the future, how we might determine what statues should be erected, and in what places, to commemorate the various people it might be appropriate to acknowledge.
I think all of us have a sense of history. It is important in giving direction to future Parliaments that we have the aspirations of all Members and that we derive some guidance and direction from what has taken place in the past. Let me refer to some unhappy historical anecdotes concerning commemorative statues. You may know, Sir, that Sir John A. Macdonald went through a great deal of trial and tribulation and it took many months and years before he was able to satisfy the appropriate acknowledgement that should have been made to Sir George Etienne Cartier. That example should give us cause to reflect on what we are doing to ensure that the procedures we follow are those that can be agreed upon and would be in place not only with respect to the motion today but forever and a day.
I think you will recall the late Judy LaMarsh when she was Secretary of State, Mr. Speaker. She placed before this House, and appropriate committees, suggestions that there be statues erected to four personalities. After many months and many years she was only successful in acquiring an agreement and acknowledgement of the kind of statue and siteing with respect to two Prime Ministers. Her other two proposals foundered and there were unhappy consequences as a result of those debates.

January 19, 1987
Parliament Hill
You will know, Mr. Speaker, that in the past the Minister of Public Works has been responsible for making suggestions concerning the identity of persons who should be acknowledged in the manner that Mr. Diefenbaker was acknowledged. I have no hesitation in suggesting to Hon. Members that my predecessors and the Departmental staff have done a superior job in that regard. Having said that, I think as a Member of Parliament and as the responsible Minister that it is appropriate that in future, all Members have more say in what should be done in matters of this kind.
I recognize that the McGrath Report contained a recommendation that Members of Parliament have a greater say over the physical precincts of Parliament. The Government's reply to that report agreed that the grounds of Parliament should be the subject of debate by the appropriate committees of both Houses. In that regard, I would recommend that the Board of Internal Economy be an adjudicator or abitrator of decisions of the kind we are now discussing. I recommend as well that consultation be had with the Boards of Internal Economy of both Houses with a view to securing an appropriate agreement about the way to proceed.
We are discussing the merit of the proposal with respect to Mr. Pearson who has indeed been acknowledged by having his name appended to an airport, a university and a building in Ottawa. Indeed, his name has been appended to an annual charity baseball game between the Expos and the Blue Jays. It is obviously a common sentiment among Canadians, no matter of which Party, that he is deserving of appropriate recognition. However, there are other people and there are other Prime Ministers.
Sir John Thompson and Prime Minister Borden were both Nova Scotians of note. Sir Charles Tupper was a Father of Confederation. They have not been acknowledged in the way suggested.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had a little trouble following the Minister's logic. As far as I know, the Board of Internal Economy has no responsibility over the grounds of Parliament.
I would like to say a few words about this matter because I support the idea that a man of the stature of Mike Pearson be recognized for his contribution, not only to Canada but to the world. Twenty-two years ago I was living in New Zealand at the time the maple leaf flag was first flown. Incidentally, it was flown in New Zealand about 15 hours before it was flown in Canada. The High Commission in Wellington had the first flag that went up at dawn on that day that flags were raised around the world. It was with a great burst of pride that I saw that symbol, which had already become a symbol of Canada even before it was the flag of Canada. I felt then and I feel now that, to a great extent, it was a symbol of Mike Pearson. I know it was called Pearson's flag, along with other names at that time. It was a flag which symbolized Prime Minister Pearson's commitment to Canada.
Prime Minister Pearson was a world statesman. As has been mentioned, he was mainly responsible for the easing of the Suez crisis in 1956. As well, he was mainly responsible for the introduction of the peace-keeping force into the Middle East during that period of crisis. For these international activities he received the Nobel Prize. The Nobel Prize citation described Mike Pearson, the diplomat, the statesman and the man, as being a man who had strong faith in the final victory of the goodness of life.
January 19, 1987

His concern for peace and his international understanding remained with him throughout his life as Prime Minister. He stood up to President Johnson during the Vietnam war. He suggested to President Johnson that it would be a good idea to cease bombing North Vietnam. As you can imagine, President Johnson was not particularly appreciative of Canada's position in that case.
I must also say that as the Leader of a minority Government in 1963 and 1965 his Government produced, with the help of the current number two Party in Canada, some very powerful social legislation. The Canada Pension Plan was established. Medicare was not completed during that period of time but the start was made. The Canada Assistance Plan was completed. His commitment to Canadian unity was expressed in the formation of the commission on bilingualism and the first real move to make the Civil Service bilingual. He believed in Canada. He believed in the world. In his life as a politican and statesman he made sure that Canada's position in the world was a major position, as did Mr. Diefenbaker whom we have recognized with a statue. Mr. Pearson did not in any way tarnish the image of Canada. Because of his contribution, and on behalf of my Party, I support the raising of a statue to honour Mike Pearson, a former Prime Minister of Canada.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   RIGHT HONOURABLE LESTER B. PEARSON STATUE TO HONOUR HIS MEMORY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to add a few comments relating to the motion put forward by my colleague for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria). But I would like first to extend to you and to all Members of this House my best wishes for a Happy and Healthy New Year.

This motion is commendable. I agree with what the Minister said in a general context about wanting to set up a committee to look at this kind of suggestion in the future. I recall last September when we unveiled the statue of John George Diefenbaker. It was rather exciting when the Chief revisited Parliament Hill. People from across the country gathered in front of the Centre Block. It was a very important occasion, not just in his memory, but for the people of this country. I recall as we stood there that the sun suddenly broke through the clouds and there he was in his bronze splendour back on Parliament Hill. I want to congratulate the Member's concern for the tremendous amount of work they put into that project, particularly the Hon. Member for Scarborough Centre (Mrs. Browes).
The special committee on reform of this House drew a lot of attention to the interest of parliamentarians from all Parties in having a greater role in directing some of the physical aspects of Parliament Hill, our workplace. I might add that the report also underlined that we should have more imput in the decision-making process involved in governing this country. We have made some strides in that area, but we have to keep
Parliament Hill
going forward, continually indicating to this House and the Government the importance of that spirit of reform.
However, the precincts of Parliament are something very special, not only to those of us who work and admire our great surroundings but for all Canadians. The National Capital Region, as you know, Sir, is where I was born and brought up. It is a piece of real estate that I am very proud to represent. I must say Ottawa is probably the most beautiful city in all of Canada. Tourism is a major industry here. It has tremendous potential to become even greater. Erecting statues to great Canadians is a way to recognize our history and make Canadians even more proud. The Mayor of Ottawa, Jim Durrell, the Chairman of the regional Government, Andy Hayden, and the Chairman of the NCC are continually meeting to focus on the priorities and objectives involved in enhancing the tourism potential of the nation's capital.
The precincts of Parliament, as I am sure you will agree, need a little bit of maintenance. We have seen a lot of deterioration in the doors, some of the gates and some of the steps. We as Members want to have more input into what this place looks like. That includes statues and commemoratives of all kinds. I am thinking of paintings and busts of great Canadians. I think of medallions honouring Governor Generals or Chief Justices and other eminent Canadians who, as the Minister mentioned, contributed significantly to Canada over the years. This includes Mr. Pearson, and we all recognize that quite clearly.
The Minister suggested that we look at these in the broad sense and that perhaps the Board of Internal Economy is one of the committees on the Hill which could look at this. As you know, it is an all-Party committee with input on a regular basis from all Members on all sides of the House.
We learned a lot from the work that was done in the last year and a half to put up the statue to Mr. Diefenbaker. We want to capitalize on that knowledge. However, I sense that cannot be done on an ad hoc basis. So I think it is time to sit down and determine a proper framework, within the parliamentary precincts, which will allow us to work together to create the commemorative objects we wish to have on Parliament Hill.
The Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) referred to a statue commissioned to honour Prime Minister Arthur Meighen. He mentioned that the family was not too pleased with the outcome. That is a fact. The statue has been in hiding for decades; that is regrettable. That is why I think the Minister focused on the importance of creating standards to be use for all future statues or other objects commissioned by Parliament to commemorate great Canadians. We must have some kind of quality control, shall we say, over the designs so that we do not have a statue sitting somewhere collecting dust. Indeed, the statue of Arthur Meighen is around somewhere. No one seems to know where, so it is obviously very well hidden.

January 19, 1987
Parliament Hill
As you know, Sir, we are running out of space within the parliamentary precincts. Land is now at a premium. I would ask you, Sir, and other Members of the House, indeed people who live within the National Capital Region and people from all over the country, to suggest locations within the National Capital Region, whether it be on this side of the river-

-or on the other side-in the Gatineau, Hull or Aylmer area-in the National Capital area, we are anxious to have input from both sides of the river on that initiative.
The Minister mentioned that there are a number of buildings including a college and the External Affairs building named after Lester B. Pearson. This is indeed a tribute to a man who enhanced Canada's international reputation. He loved baseball and the annual game between the Blue Jays and the Montreal Expos is named after him. I understand that this year they have been unable to find a date suitable to both teams and the game may not be played.
The Minister is suggesting that a more comprehensive approach be taken, one totally free of any partisan considerations. We must consider the requirements of parliamentarians, the Board of Internal Economy, the National Capital Region, Ministers and Prime Ministers. We would like to see certain parts of our past properly reconstructed and located. We speak these days of the ceremonial route, a very important project which will make our capital city unique in the world. Our scenic route will have beautiful views of Parliament Hill and the museums which are presently being built. As well, it will have statues of some of our great Canadians. We hope to have a statue built to honour Lester B. Pearson which will eventually be placed somewhere within the parliamentary precincts or along the ceremonial route where proud Canadians can see it and remember that Lester B. Pearson contributed significantly to make our country one of the best in the world in which to live.
I support the Minister's general proposal to enhance the role of the Board of Internal Economy. I also support the initiative of the Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell. I hope he will continue to persist to ensure that this becomes a priority within the new over-all comemorative framework which the Minister hopes to see parliamentarians and parliamentary assistants focus upon to make a lasting tribute to a man who was, without question, an effective Prime Minister and a great Canadian.

speechtext:
Those words of Lester Pearson describe the great relationship which existed between him and his constituents in Algoma East.
After hearing the speech of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mclnnes) I am not exactly sure what the policy of the Government is with regard to the placement of statues in commemoration of the memory of great Prime Ministers of our country. However, statues of all Prime Ministers since 1920 have been erected. I felt it was fitting that last fall we erected a statue of Mr. Diefenbaker, a great Prime Minister. It would be fitting to do the same now in respect of Mr. Pearson. It is absolutely essential that that be done with a non-partisan and positive approach, as it was done with regard to Mr. Diefenbaker.
The Minister's policy seems rather fuzzy to me. He suggested that perhaps there should be more input, as recommended by the McGrath committee, into the activities and decisions relating to Parliament Hill. Surely there can be no more active way for Members of Parliament to participate in decisions relating to Parliament Hill than to move a motion during Private Member's Hour and give every Member an opportunity to participate fully in the debate. If the Minister is proposing an over-all policy which will allow Mr. Pearson's statue to be established on Parliament Hill on the same basis as Mr. Diefenbaker's statue, I think that is a workable arrangement. However, if it is strictly an approach to frustrate the establishment of a statue to honour Mr. Pearson, I think it is a less than acceptable way for the Minister to proceed.
I am sure that Lester B. Pearson qualifies to meet whatever the requirements would be to have a statue raised in his honour on Parliament Hill. Few if any Canadians have made such an outstanding contribution in international affairs for our country and for the world, in domestic and social legislation or in human terms which we in Algoma and Algoma East appreciate so much.
I want to indicate in the strongest possible way my support for the establishment of this statue commemorating the tremendous contribution of the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson to Parliament and to our country.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   RIGHT HONOURABLE LESTER B. PEARSON STATUE TO HONOUR HIS MEMORY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate being recognized during this Private Members' Hour. I had no intention of speaking in this debate because I expected that things would go much as they did a year ago when the motion came forward for a statue to be erected in honour of John G. Diefenbaker. As the Public Works critic I was alerted by my House Leader to be ready to speak. However, a colleague had indicated he would like to speak on this matter and I bowed to him because I thought this motion would receive smooth passage through the House. However, once the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mclnnes) made his remarks, I must say, quite frankly, I was aroused to speak.
Parliament Hill
The Minister of Public Works said that before a statute could be erected to Mr. Pearson, a former Prime Minister of this country, the matter would have to be referred to a committee to set up guidelines and to go through a long and studied procedure. This strikes me as rather strange. If this is to be the approach, then it should have been taken before the decision was made to erect the statue to John Diefenbaker. A year ago a Private Members' Motion passed through this House to honour the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker, a former Prime Minister of Canada, and rightly so, and the statue has been erected. If the Government wanted to take the approach of setting up guidelines, it should have done so before that statue was erected.
What arouses me, Mr. Speaker, is that what we seem to have here is a petty partisan approach to the question of honouring a former Prime Minister. Is the Government just putting road blocks in the way because it is a former Liberal Prime Minister the private Member is asking to have honoured? If we chose to honour John Diefenbaker then why not honour Mr. Pearson? Certainly, their contribution to history and to our country is of equal merit. Surely most Canadians associate John George Diefenbaker and Lester B. Pearson together in Government.
I was surprised that the Minister of Public Works would speak in this Chamber during Private Members' Hour in order to throw cold water on a motion by a private Member to honour a former Prime Minister. I would have thought he would have waited to hear full debate, allowing private Members to make this decision. I want to make it clear that I think there is a need for a vote on this particular motion. It is sad and regrettable that there is a need for a vote. This motion should have been supported without question. However, because of the comments made by the Minister of Public Works, I feel there is a need for a vote and for private Members to be able to express their opinion and not be whipped into line by the Minister of Public Works.
I want to keep my comments brief, so I will just say that not only was Mr. Pearson Prime Minister in the same historical period as Mr. Diefenbaker, whom we have already honoured, but Mr. Pearson did make significant contributions to this country. He won the Nobel Peace Prize, so obviously he was honoured internationally. He had a part to play in the establishment of medicare and the establishment of the Canada Pension Plan, both of which were significant policy initiatives for a Canadian Prime Minister to have been involved in.
So as not to limit the opportunity of other Hon. Members to express their opinion on this question, and so as not to lose the opportunity to have a vote, I will bring my comments quickly to a close by saying that it strikes me as being partisan that a Minister of the Crown would suggest a different procedure regarding a statue honouring Mr. Pearson than that which was followed for the erection of a statue to honour Mr. Diefenbaker.

January 19, 1987
Parliament Hill

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will not impede the Hon. Member. I recognize the instinctive intuitive premonition in your earlier remark, Mr. Speaker, and we will hang in together.
I had a feeling of great pleasure some months ago to sit on the platform when we dedicated a statue to the Right Hon. John George Diefenbaker. I had the honour of serving in this House both in opposition and on the Government side when Mr. Diefenbaker was Prime Minister and then Leader of the Opposition.
Our quarter of the House thought it entirely appropriate that Mr. Diefenbaker's historical position in Canada in his role as leader of our country should be recognized in a permanent way on Parliament Hill. We looked at it in a non-partisan fashion. Therefore, I rise very briefly to say that I hope the Minister and Hon. Members on all sides of the House will afford the same distinction to Mr. Pearson who, as my friend from the New Democratic Party has remarked, occupied the stage in this House at the same time as Mr. Diefenbaker. They sat opposite each other, on both sides of the House, during a very remarkable period of Canadian history.
I think the arguments put forward in honour of Mr. Diefenbaker some time ago-and I congratulated the mover of that particular motion-apply equally to this motion. I would hope we would have unanimous approval of this motion so that the two men who faced each other so actively across the House representing, as they saw it, our country, would be able to face each other, perhaps at some distance, across Parliament Hill.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   RIGHT HONOURABLE LESTER B. PEARSON STATUE TO HONOUR HIS MEMORY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I certainly respect the thoughts of the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) and his concurrence that our former Prime Ministers, John George Diefenbaker and Lester B. Pearson, deserve to be honoured within a short time of each other. It is the same situation as it existed 11 years ago when the late Prime Ministers Mackenzie King and Louis St. Laurent were also honoured with statues.
The late Mr. Pearson was a man of outstanding abilities. During his time he was greatly honoured. However, he also created a certain amount of divisiveness. It has taken the last
20 years to accept his good works, something for which he is highly respected. We know that he will go down in history as an outstanding statesman. There is a place for a statue of Mr. Pearson to be erected here on Parliament Hill. But where is that place?
It is true that we erected a statue of John G. Diefenbaker, something which was long overdue. That former Prime Minister captured the imagination of every Canadian. He was one of the great Canadians in the history of our country. He led a strong Government and a strong Opposition. He was highly respected right up until his last days in power.

speechtext: Was not Mr. Pearson?

speechtext:
Mr. Pearson was as well. I thank the Hon. Member for his prompting. I realize that we are talking about Mr. Pearson.
Until the unveiling of the commemorative statue of the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker this fall some 11 years had passed since the erection of the previous two statues. There is a sculptor in Edmonton, Mr. Negritto, who is a near-genious. He has extraordinary ability. He has made representations to the Government in this view. There is also a sculptor of outstanding ability in Winnipeg, Mr. Mall. Undoubtedly, there are other sculptors with outstanding abilities who are willing to offer sculptures of the type we would like to see on the grounds of Parliament Hill. However, the question remains, where should they be placed?
At the moment there are four statues on the grounds. They are statues of the former Prime Ministers Borden, King, St. Laurent and Diefenbaker. They are in places which were thought to be relevant at the time. Is this the way in which statues honouring the leaders of our country should be located? What about busts? There has been talk of paintings and pictures. Now we hear talk of standing memorabilia. What will we do with such memorabilia? Is there some overall plan? We have just erected a statue to an outstanding Canadian. Should we rush in and erect another statue on the hallowed grounds of Parliament Hill? The Government feels that we should stop and consider. After all, only a few months have passed since the last statue was erected. We must consider what the best method is for locating sculptures of this type.
One of the problems we have had in the past is that we have forgotten the history of our country. We were not even taught the history of our country. When I went to school I learned British, French and European history but very little about Canadian history. The tables have been turned. We now think about our Canadian history. We think about the impact the French had when they came here over 300 years ago. We think about the English who travelled all over the country and who finally ruled it. What about Canadians since 1867 and the years since? Have we really learned the history of our country? The history of our country should be reflected on
January 19, 1987

Parliament Hill in a more orderly fashion to reflect what is important in terms of what has occurred.
As we consider the possibility of erecting another sculpture we must consider where it should be placed. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mclnnes) has said that we should create an orderly plan and have a study made of this matter. In this way the erection of sculptures could be presented for the best interests and delight of all Canadians, as well as for the enjoyment of visitors who come from other countries. In this way they will see that we have some rhyme and reason in terms of the placement of our statues. We must consider how they can be enjoyed and whether they meet the needs of families and parliamentarians. These questions should be considered before we rush into erecting another statue on Parliament Hill.
