speechtext:
I regret to interrupt the Hon. Member, but the hour provided for the consideration of Private Members' Business has now expired. Pursuant to Standing Order 36(2) this order shall be dropped to the bottom of the order of precedence. However, I should advise Hon. Members that there is some possibility that the motion will be scheduled for debate again on Tuesday, February 10. In view of representations which have been made I wish to bring this matter to the attention of Hon. Members.
The House will now move to Government Orders.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Miss Carney that Bill C-37, an Act respecting the imposition of a charge on the export of certain softwood lumber products, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee, and the amendment of Mr. Turner (Vancouver Quadra), (p. 2382).

Mr. Speaker, I am very proud this evening to be the second hitter at bat for the Government on the proposed legislation dealing with the export tax and the American countervailing duty. I am particularly pleased to follow another British Columbian, the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney), who has carried the ball very well with respect to this issue. British Columbians are proud of the fact that she listened to Premier Vander Zalm of B.C. and the people of B.C., including the IWA, and not Adam Zimmerman of Noranda in Toronto or Premier Peterson of Ontario.
Softwood Lumber Products Export Charge Act
I am particularly pleased to stand here this evening because my region is so dependent upon the forest industry. Some
7.000	to 8,000 workers are directly involved in the forest industry in Nanaimo and Alberni, British Columbia. Some
20.000	to 25,000 people are involved in the secondary industries which rely on forestry. Port Alberni in my riding was the forestry capital of Canada in 1986. Thus I would like to say a few words about this proposed legislation.
I was in British Columbia when this deal, as it has been called, was signed. I talked to the forest workers in the province. The message they asked me to bring back to Ottawa was to tell the Chicken Littles that the sky is not falling. This is not the end of the forest industry in British Columbia, or in Canada. British Columbians realize that we have not been replanting what we have been cutting down. They look forward to the fact that we will actually have some money for reforestation in our province and across the country. The province supports what we are doing, as do the forestry unions.
I think it is important to read into the record a couple of paragraphs of the position taken by the International Woodworkers of America in British Columbia. In a letter to the Minister for International Trade they state:
The International Woodworkers of America wishes to extend its general support for the recent negotiated settlement of the softwood lumber dispute with the United States.
Under ideal conditions, many of us would have preferred to have our "day in court" in order to try to reduce the 15 per cent preliminary duty imposed by the U.S. Commerce Department last October. However, given the realities of the strong protectionist mood in the United States, it is extremely unlikely that the 15 per cent could have been reduced substantially in the final Commerce Department decision.
And even if the correct duty were eventually determined to be lower than 15 per cent, that decision could only be arrived at through three or four years of protracted court proceedings. In the meantime, all of the revenues from the countervailing duty would continue to flow into U.S. government coffers at the rate of 12 per cent to 15 per cent on the selling price of lumber.
Those revenues properly belong to the owners of the trees-the people of British Columbia and Canada. We therefore strongly believe that it was absolutely essential to conclude a negotiated settlement with the United States which will guarantee that the increased taxes on softwood lumber shipments to the United States be kept in Canada.
This is the IWA talking. This is a union that represents the men and women who work in the forests of B.C. and across the country. This is a responsible position taken by a responsible union that has entered the 1980s. What does the Opposition and some of the media have to say? The sky is falling. Hundreds of mills are going to shut down. Thousands of jobs will disappear.
Well, we went through all of that with the shake and shingle affair last year and we know the reality of that. The NDP and the Liberals said then that it was the end of the industry; thousands of British Columbians would be on the dole. Now eight months later, thanks to market forces and good management, the shake and shingle industry in this country is doing very well. That was a 35 per cent tariff. Here we are talking about a 15 per cent export tax. When it comes to opposition

January 19, 1987
Softwood Lumber Products Export Charge Act
criticism, that is basically old wine in a new bottle. Come to think of it, all that the Opposition is good at is whining. Nobody whines better than the NDP and the Liberals.
I have a comment from Frank Beban of Beban Logging in Nanaimo. He told me that he does not think the export tax will have that much of an effect; it should not be detrimental to the industry. He feels that the value of the Canadian dollar will have more effect on the B.C. forest industry. This is the same Frank Beban who, with Western Forest Products, was fighting to save logging jobs on the Queen Charlotte Islands. That is where the NDP believe that trees grow to the sky and then suddenly fall down on their own, and that they should not be chopped down by these horrible loggers. That is where they tried to block the logging on Lyell Island. One of the federal NDP Members even dressed up as a Haida native to try and stop the logging. Today they are coming across as the great defenders of the loggers of British Columbia. They are very concerned about the jobs of British Columbians. Horse nonsense, or better still, horse sense.
I see that the Liberal Member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Turner) is here. To his credit he travelled up to the Queen Charlottes and saw the Lyell Island situation. He made quite an effort on the Jack Webster Show, and in the House, about the indiscriminate logging of those horrible forest companies. Those are the same forest companies that create the docks, the roads, provide emergency medical service to the people in the Queen Charlottes and throughout British Columbia, and have built up the infrastructure that we are so dependent upon. Now I see this afternoon the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition trying to hoist this Bill for six months. How can you go back to British Columbia, sir, and tell them that $400 million of reforestation money is going to be delayed for six months? That is about $200 million that they will not get. They will get it down the road.
American protectionism is real and ugly, there is no doubt about that. Let us look at some of the facts of this legislation and what has happened as far as the background is concerned. In 1982-83 a countervailing petition similar to this one was launched by the American forest industry. At that time 29 per cent of the U.S. market was ours. That caused a great deal of fear in British Columbia. Fortunately, at that time the decision was in our favour. But times have changed since then. The forest industry was saying that we won it in 1983, and we will win it in 1986. We are talking about 1986-87 in North America and times have changed. We have gone from some 19 per cent of the American market 10 years ago to some 35, 36 per cent now, some say it is perhaps even higher. The Canadian dollar is devalued even more. In the same 10-year span that the Canadian dollar went from $1.04 down to about 73 cents our share of the American market went from some 19 per cent to 35 or 36 per cent.
Anybody who has talked to American politicians can understand why they have been upset. They stand in their own ridings and watch carload after carload of Canadian lumber going across the border while their own lumber workers are
lined up at the unemployment insurance offices. Any politician in this Chamber will understand the sentiments of the American politicians. It has become more real and ugly over the passing years.
In the summer of 1985 I travelled to Washington, D.C. with an all-parliamentary delegation. The Members for Skeena (Mr. Fulton), Capilano (Mrs. Collins), and Prince George- Peace River (Mr. Oberle) who is now the Minister of Science and Technology, were in attendance. We learned there how real that protectionism sentiment is. Even if the countervailing duty failed, we were told that they were prepared to introduce an omnibus Bill that would take action against our forest products. The only light on the horizon in the U.S., even back in 1985, was that we had a good product that American home builders and home buyers wanted. As a matter of fact, one of the southern Senators said to us that at church on Sunday he was doing the lay sermon. As he walked in the front door a representative of the southern forest industry was saying, "For goodness sake, nail those Canadians. You have got to stop those Canadians". After the sermon he walked out the back door and there was a contractor who builds houses in Georgia saying, "Lay off the Canadians. We need their product. We like their product". That is the type of turmoil we have been going through over the years.
Anyone who has talked to the forest workers, the legislators, or the industry knows that there has been very real concern. Even early in 1986 the forest industry told us as the Government of Canada, "Hands off. Let us deal with it. We won it before, we will win it again". But then by August of 1986 the political pressures in the U.S. were realized, not only by us but by the forest industry in Canada. The provinces, labour, and the forest industry urged that we negotiate our way out of this particular mess. That is why our Minister of International Trade offered a 10 per cent presentation to the Americans to try to forgo the preliminary determination on the countervailing duty. As we all know, that offer was refused.
In October we lost the battle but not the war, in our opinion. When that 15 per cent preliminary determination came down there was a great deal of consternation in the industry and the Government. We thought we could find a way out of it. That is why in November, at the First Ministers' Conference in Vancouver, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), the Minister of International Trade, the Minister of State for Forestry and Mines (Mr. Merrithew), and the Premiers of this country, with one exception, managed to find a consensus and make another offer to the Americans that would hopefully keep the money north of the 49th Parallel. On December 30 our negotiations were successful.
What did the negotiations entail? The Americans wanted a $1.1 billion increase in stumpage. They wanted an outright veto in changes to our stumpage system. They wanted the export tax to apply to the added value of our lumber. They wanted prohibition against our forestry companies using the cost of the export tax as a business deduction, as they do with stumpage now. They got none of those demands, not one.
January 19, 1987

Instead, on December 30 our Government was successful in ensuring that the $600 million in reforestation money stayed north of the 49th Parallel. Now we will replant what we harvest.
That has been the position of the B.C. NDP for years. They have demanded that we farm and not mine the resource. That is a position that many B.C. Members of Parliament can agree with. It is ironic that now, thanks to a Progressive Conservative national Government, we will be able to do that in my home Province of British Columbia and across the country.
I have some concerns about how these windfall dollars will be spent. Much of it relies on trust with the provinces. We have no real assurances that every penny, with the exception of the cost of administration of the export tax, will go into planting trees, weeding, spacing, and thinning, and doing the job we have not done up until now. But it is essentially a provincial resource. So there will be a great deal of trust involved here.
If I may turn to a few media reports on the imposition of the export tax, let me start with the media in Nanaimo-Alberni, the forestry capital of Canada. The Alberni Valley Times states: "Export duty reasonable-under the circumstances".
Ottawa's export duty saved a lot of money for Canada that would have been spent in the U.S. had not the federal and provincial Governments negotiated the compromise with the tariff-hungry Americans.
Turning to the Nanaimo Daily Free Press of January 3, it reads:
While forest industry unions appear to welcome that lumber export tax agreement with the U.S., it's the big timber bosses' turn to be moaning the odds.
That 15 per cent added cost has produced long faces and fairly scathing criticism of the deal, which was worked out just hours before the deadline-
It continues:
Had there been no agreement, Canada could have faced a tariff even higher than the 15 per cent now agreed.
The difference is that the 15 per cent stays on this side of the 49th parallel. On BCTV, on December 31, an announcer said:
NDP Trade Critic Bob Williams says the softwood accord is "a pretty good deal".
In his interview, Mr. Williams said:
That's right. I'm afraid I disagree (with Broadbent). He is rightly concerned about the sovereignty issue. But at the same time the provinces have not been collecting the value of the trees. I think Mr. Broadbent is ignoring that side of the equation.
I think these articles should be brought to light, in that the Opposition seems to put so much credence upon what the media has to say on these issues. In the January 8 edition of The Toronto Sun, the following article appeared:
In the case of softwood lumber, the American buyers are clearly calling the shots. But not all of them. One irony is that the new 15 per cent export tax imposed here will probably be reflected in higher home prices in the U.S. as importers pass on higher costs to the American consumer.
Which is, if you think about it, a delicious irony.
Softwood Lumber Products Export Charge Act
Then the writer continued:
Meantime, there is no cause for panic. Martin Brian Mulroney hasn't "sold out" the country, nor is he likely to. Peace, order and good government will prevail. The sun will rise in the east and set in the opposite direction.
Life will go on.
Then the following appeared in The Sault Star of Sault Ste. Marie:
It is interesting to note that one Canadian group with a major stake in the issue, the International Woodworkers of America, supports the agreement as "the lesser of the two evils".
In The Toronto Sun Peter Worthington wrote the following:
I wonder if our "nationalists" would prefer the money going to the U.S. in the form of a tariff rather than staying here as tax revenue? Would that be a sell-out too?
Also Worthington wrote:
-one wonders how Canada is supposed to "stand up to" or "resist" American pressure in free-trade talks? Surely with a spirit of isolationism and protectionism rampant in the U.S., it is imperative that we get a free-trade deal as quickly as we can,-
Also he went on to write:
It serves little purpose to reduce the dispute into a "who won, who lost" contest. Free trade is not a hockey game-it's our future. And it seems that on this one, Canada is ahead of the rest of the country.-
They go on and on, including the article written by Marjorie Nichols in The Vancouver Sun which read:
There is nothing novel about this agreement. In terms of the monitoring and enforcement procedures, it is less intrusive into Canadian affairs than other bilateral and multilateral agreements.
The 15 per cent countervail duty is gone, hundreds of millions of dollars in reforestation have been made available, and Canadian sovereignty has been maintained. When one enters into any agreement, there is some give and take on both sides. We have plenty of examples of that. The Auto Pact is one. The Pacific Salmon Treaty is another. The Columbia River Treaty is another example of give and take on both sides. We are giving the U.S.A. a 15 per cent export tax, and they are taking away the countervailing duty which it had imposed.
Let us be realistic and grown up about this. Sovereignty is not the issue. The give and take of any negotiating procedure is a fact of life. When we talk about sovereignty, let us remember what Ambassador Niles had to say in his statement of January
2:
The United States Government will not be concerned with how Canadian authorities make changes in their forest management practices. When they do so or what form these changes make. These are matters for Canadians to decide.
The point the Opposition seems to be missing is that if we had allowed the countervailing duty, Canadian jobs may well have been affected anyway. With the export tax, we will be creating hundreds of jobs in reforestation in the country. Much of the cost of the export tax will be borne by the Americans as well.
The price of Canadian lumber in the U.S. has gone up since December 30. At the end of 1986 it was $190 per thousand for two by four lumber; today it is up to $202, a rise of some $12 in the cost of Canadian lumber in the U.S. It is already being

January 19, 1987
Softwood Lumber Products Export Charge Act
borne by the American consumer. It shows how tariffs and countervailing duties cannot benefit anybody, except perhaps Governments or politicians; they do not benefit the average consumer. That is what free trade is all about. We are trying to get rid of these irritants and ensure that we have the kind of co-operation we need.
As the Minister already mentioned earlier today, the value of stock in Canadian forest companies has gone up, not down. It has gone up since the export tax was introduced, so we can be Chicken Littles or optimistic Canadians.
It is my opinion that this legislation will stand the test of time. The provinces retain their flexibility in determining stumpage pricing, a dangerous development in U.S. countervail policy has been avoided by the withdrawal of the petition, and the ability of the provinces to determine their own natural resource management policies remains unimpaired. They are all worthy goals and accomplishments of which the Government and the House can be proud.
The Canadian forest industry will survive this latest attack by the Americans. We have had them before; hopefully we will not have them again. Our forest industry may even be better managed for what has happened, better managed because of the export tax and the American countervailing duty petition.
We will always have a quality Canadian product which Americans want to buy, so the sky is not falling. It has in fact brightened. I ask that we pass this piece of legislation at the earliest possible opportunity.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a question of my hon. friend who just made a very eloquent plea for support of the Government's initiative.
I should like to refer him to a quotation of Mr. J. Martig-nago, one of the chief officers of Balco Industries, a major forest producer in central British Columbia. I want to take just a moment to quote what he said:
The 15 per cent export tax is devastating. It could cost Balco approximately $8 million per annum.
We will be down sooner and for longer. The Forest Industry Council estimates the additional cost to the Canadian industry will be $600 million per year. That is well in excess of the total profit of all lumber companies in Canada.
The Government ended up giving us Hobson's choice-either the tax goes into our pockets or theirs. What would really hurt is if the language prevents the use of the tax to enhance the forest resource base.
The countervailing duty must remain as a tax on the product exported to the U.S. Were the tax applied on the basis of log scale as stumpage the entire production of every company would be adversely affected. This in effect would not only impact the U.S. market but also eliminate the possibility for Canadian firms to diversify and service international markets other than the U.S.
The Hon. Member's presentation was an interesting one. Although I disagree with it, it contained some interesting arguments. Does he disagree with the comments of this very respected, well-known authority on the British Columbia interior forestry industry when he said that the 15 per cent export tax was devasting?

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to receive a question from the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis). It was not that long ago, about 10 years, that I was a young radio station cub reporter and the Hon. Member was an alderman in Kamloops and was beginning his political career. If I only knew then what I know now, Mr. Speaker. However, I am pleased to receive a question from him.
Once again we obviously have a divergent point of view. For every letter or comment that he pulls out, I can pull out one with the opposite point of view. Again we have some statistics of doom and gloom; they seem to get used to that in the Opposition. It is full of could, should, maybe and if.
The same is true if we look through Hansard in May 1986 when we dealt with the shake and shingle industry-it could cost, it might cost, or it might have to shut down, not very much of which came true.
I prefer to believe that the country has received sort of a gift from the U.S.A. in reforestation dollars which we can use to the benefit of our forest industry. I prefer to believe that we are going to create more jobs in reforestation, in weeding, spacing and thinning than may be lost in the mills and the forests of British Columbia.
The cost of S600 million has been pulled out of the air. I have heard other costs as well. I know one cost for sure. We will receive those hundreds of millions of export tax dollars into our reforestation funding.
Do I disagree with what the Hon. Member has to say? Time will tell whether the Hon. Member is right or I am right. Perhaps with our mutual experience in the B.C. forest industry and its implications, I prefer to believe that the government Member is right and the opposition Member is wrong.

Mr. Speaker, can the Hon. Member direct any Member of this House to a document or a public statement or anything when he says that hundreds of millions of windfall dollars will come to B.C. and that they will be spent on reforestation? In fact, the Premier of British Columbia has said quite the opposite, that the money will be used for things other than forestry. Can the Hon. Member direct anyone in this House to any document or any statement saying that that money will be spent on reforestation, or is that just pie in the sky?

It is an accepted fact, Mr. Speaker, that the Province of British Columbia, along with the Province of Quebec, were anticipating raising their stumpage fees well in advance of what has been going on over the past few months. It is the Premier of British Columbia, let us not forget, who initiated the negotiations, along with our Minister for International Trade and the other provincial premiers, to try to bring in that export tax and to keep it in place. As I said earlier, a lot of this is based on trust, accommodation and belief.
January 19, 1987

We have met with Premier Vander Zalm twice since he attained office in the fall of 1986. I would put forward to this House that the Premier of British Columbia will do everything he can to ensure that the $400 million in British Columbia is put into reforestation. The Premier is not sure that he can spend all of that in one year, which shows the kind of windfall dollars that are involved. The Premier of B.C. has said, I believe, as reported in the Vancouver Sun, that when it comes to a choice between growing a tree, if he uses the funds, and saving a patient who has heart trouble, then that is a decision he will have to make at that time. I am trusting, as we should trust, that he will make the right decision when the time comes.

Mr. Speaker, since this is a bad tax, badly applied, does the Member believe that the bad application of the tax should be sustained or not? I gather from the Member's speech that he endorses the Government's decision to impose the tax.
Is the Hon. Member aware that stumpage in the Province of Quebec, for example, is very substantially higher per thousand cubic feet or per cubic metre than it is in the Province of British Columbia? Is it fair that the tax should apply at the same rate in Quebec as it does in British Columbia?
Is the Hon. Member aware that the tax to be applied is on the f.o.b. price at the mill and as a consequence it will be applied on the f.o.b. price of something like $230 per thousand cubic feet in Quebec as compared to $160 per thousand cubic feet in the interior of British Columbia? In other words, the tax will wind up being about $10 per thousand cubic feet higher in Quebec than it is in British Columbia. Is that fair? Is that just, and if not, what does the Hon. Member intend to do with it as a member of the governing Party?

Mr. Speaker, that is not a certainty. The Hon. Member speaks with great certainty that it is going to be an unfair tax applied in different regions of the country. We do not know that for sure. Those negotiations are still going on right now between our Minister for International Trade and the Premiers and forestry Ministers across Canada.
Oh, oh!

What a delightful laugh the Hon. Member has. There is no certainty at all of how it will be applied, whether or not it will be higher in Quebec or lower in British Columbia. That is what the negotiations are all about. That is what the NDP does not seem to understand.
It is in the Bill.
Negotiations, thank goodness, are being done by a Progressive Conservative Government and not an NDP Government.

Mr. Speaker, I have another question for the Hon. Member. He will be well aware that on the question regarding
Softwood Lumber Products Export Charge Act
sovereignty, to which he referred in his presentation, when you look at the actual agreement it states:
-that Canada may reduce or eliminate the export charge if other fees are placed on lumber production. But Canada can do this only "subject to further consultations and agreement between the two Governments".
The two Governments being the Government of the United States and the Government of Canada. The agreement is saying that unless the United States Government agrees to this change of obtaining these funds, Canada cannot proceed, the industry cannot proceed or the provincial Government cannot proceed. When it says that in the actual agreement signed by the Governments of Canada and the United States, would the Hon. Member not have to agree that it is really saying that the U.S. Government does, in fact, have a certain amount of decision making in how we manage our forest resource?

Once again, Mr. Speaker, I must repeat how happy I am that our Government is doing the negotiating around here and not the NDP.
Does the Hon. Member not realize that in other agreements we have, from the Auto Pact to the Pacific Salmon Treaty alone, there is give and take on both sides? Decisions cannot be made unilaterally by one side without affecting the other. There are agreements that involve mutual negotiation. The Americans are concerned about the arithmetic of that 15 per cent export tax, and rightfully so. They will be monitoring the situation in Canada, but under no circumstances have we given up our sovereignty, under no circumstances at all.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions and comments are now terminated. Debate. The Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau).

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-37 now before the House can be viewed from a fiscal point of view. It can have some other implications we could refer to from the legal, technical point of view, but the heart of this whole debate centers on the ability of the Government of Canada and the provincial governments to make decisions concerning the forest industry, which is a major resource. Mr. Speaker, I would say that this Bill raises two important questions-first, the integrity of our Canadian sovereignty, and second the financial situation that could be faced by a significant part of the forest industry and its workers.
Mr. Speaker, a moment ago I heard the Government Member say there had been no impairment of sovereignty because of those negotiations, and that there had to be some sort of trade-off in those negotiations. The reason why on this side of the House we feel the integrity of Canadian sovereignty has been set at stake by this Government is that we did not have a free hand. The negotiations were entered upon under duress. There was a decision by the U.S. Government, and I wish I had all the time needed to put the case of that 15 per cent levy against the fact that a country's resources may be taxed according to the country's will, and the establishment of new stumpage fees is not a subsidy to our forest industry.

January 19, 1987
Softwood Lumber Products Export Charge Act
Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the House defend that view on the authority, not of books or expert opinions but of a ruling by the U.S. International Trade Commission which made a decision on that matter in 1983. As our leader asked earlier today, what is it that has changed in that whole debate since 1982-83? Stumpage fees have remained on the whole identical, and so did their implementation. Mr. Speaker, there has been no change in the international agreements binding the various governments that are members of the GATT. What is it that has changed since 1982-83, if not a Government that cannot stand up to the U.S. Government, a Government that is ready to cave in to each and every demand being addressed to it.
I would not want to come back on the issues which have already been raised such as the national energy policy, the drug legislation, etc.: the Mulroney Government has merely caved in to each American demand and this is again the case today.
We did not negotiate freely, contrary to what the previous speaker, a Government Member, has stated, but we have been forced to enter discussion under the threat of a 15 per cent tax. And given these circumstances, the sovereignty of this country has been challenged.
The second point with which I would like to deal is that not only the integrity of Canadian sovereignty is challenged, but a major Canadian industry could be disabled to the extent that several plants would have to close and their employees laid off. I should like to explain to those who are listening in this House and elsewhere why we have reached that point, and why we are now discussing a bill the contents of which have been dictated by the American government. Why are we forced to discuss it in a Parliament where the various regions of the country are represented? Why do we have to deal with such legislation?
The behaviour of the Prime Minister of this country was extremely naive and lacking in sophistication when, at the Quebec Summit, without preparation of any kind, without prior debate in the House, without prior discussion with the provincial governments, without checking on the situation in the U.S. Senate, without any preparation and without any really thorough research, the Prime Minister of this country agreed to embark on free trade talks with the U.S. President.
In the fall of that year, at the beginning of the session, we were treated to a Government statement about seven or eight minutes long, and that is all we had from this Government in the House, a statement announcing that an agreement had been reached between the U.S. President and the Prime Minister of Canada on starting free trade talks. Unfortunately, the Prime Minister had forgotten that for the talks to get under way, the U.S. President had to refer back to the Senate and that a Senate committee had to approve a decision to start negotiations on the basis of the proposed fast track concept. Unfortunately, the Senate committee's decision came as a surprise to the Conservative Government. The committee refused to give its majority approval to a decision that had
been announced by our Prime Minister and the President of the United States. That is when the trouble started. To avoid losing face, the U.S. President had to do some arm twisting, and in this respect, a number of letters are often referred to.
I have one here before me, signed on May 8, 1986, in which the U.S. President thanked his friend, Dear Bob, in other words, Senator Packwood, for finally deciding to pass the resolution. But he told him he intended to put the pressure on in order to accelerate the process of settling the softwood lumber problem. That was the price that the American Government had to pay to obtain the Senate committee's agreement. If we look at the original text of what the U.S. President said to Senator Packwood-
"I intend to press for an expedited resolution to this problem independent of the comprehensive negotiations".

In addition to the U.S. President's commitment there was also a senior official with the administration's trade sector in the United States, Clayton Yeutter, who in a letter to Senator David Pryor on April 17, 1986, said, and these are his own words:

"We will get timber fixed".
[ Translation]
And that was in the context of discussing whether to go along with the plan for free trade talks between Canada and the United States. So the U.S. Senate had its arm twisted and the U.S. administration promised to foot the bill. However, in the final instance, it is Canada's softwood lumber workers who are going to pay, because as a result of the Prime Minister's incompetence and lack of foresight, we and our workers in the softwood lumber industry are going to suffer the effects of this Government's poor administration.
What happened, Mr. Speaker, was that the tax was imposed. When we were hit by the 15 per cent tax imposed by the United States, the first reaction of this Government was to panic. Why did Mr. Reagan, the friend of the Canadian Prime Minister, impose a 15 per cent tax after we had supposedly undertaken friendly discussions to solve all trade problems between our two countries? There was therefore some panic.
The first reaction of the Minister was to say: We are going to fight. We shall appeal to GATT, we shall fight to have this 15 per cent tax withdrawn which we find unjust because it goes against the rules of international trade.
The House will recall the rhetoric which was used at the press conference. The first reaction was panic. The second was agressiveness. The third reaction was to give up on everything and to make, supposedly as a final offer, a counter-proposal of 10 per cent instead of 15 per cent.
January 19, 1987

The Minister for International Trade said that this was a final offer. Not only was it not a final offer, but we had to go even further and obtain a settlement which is exactly what the Americans wanted. The Government tried to rattle its sword in this battle, but when it saw that its position was not strong enough to negotiate, it showed the white flag late in December and agreed with the American requirements and signed this agreement with which everyone is now familiar and which is reproduced nearly word for word in the Bill under consideration.
The second point I would like to raise concerns the effects of all this. Many have said how important the forest industry is for all of Canada, and as the representative of a Quebec constituency, I would like to underline this importance.
Our lumber industry includes nearly 400 businesses and 21,500 workers and its exports amount to several hundred millions and even billions of dollars. This measure will have an impact on our lumber exports since 51 per cent of Quebec production is exported to the United States.
This industry is therefore important for all of Canada and extremely important for Quebec. This is why this Bill will have a considerable impact. I have had the opportunity to discuss this issue with representatives of the industry and the reactions we have had have been extremely unfavourable. We have been told that the industry is in great difficulty.
Earlier in this debate I heard the Conservative Member and others, including the Minister, say that the price would be paid by the Americans. We have evidence from company owners who told us in no uncertain terms that the day after the tax was imposed they tried to raise their prices so as to be able to pay this tax, but they did not even sell 1,000 feet of lumber. They had to lower their prices and absorb the full tax just to maintain sales in the United States.
So until now the price or tax has been paid by Canadian companies. We would be able to make the Americans pay this tax only if the demand for timber in the United States were to soar overnight. In that case, of course, we could boost prices and make them pay part of the increase. But this surtax is levied at a time when the United States construction industry is hard hit by the tax reform. All those who followed the tax reform debate and saw the reaction of American house builders, all those people are telling us-and I heard the testimony of Americans-that as a result of tax reform amendments affecting those who buy houses or apartments for rental purposes there will be no new housing construction until an adjustment is made. In other words, for the next six to twelve months the tax will have to be paid by Canadian companies and borne by Canadian lumber industry workers.
Mr. Speaker, the consequences will be far-reaching. We could quote a number of statements by experts who commented on this question. I think you know them, including some Quebec company presidents. Then we heard the testimony of the President of the Chamber of Commerce who was also the

owner of a major industry. Their remarks have been reported in all newspapers, so I would rather not repeat them here.
Rather, I should like to use the time which I still have at my disposal to deal with the very substance of Bill C-37, examine once more the whole issue and emphasize the sovereignty aspect.
Mr. Speaker, Clause 5 provides that a charge will be imposed on a great variety of forest products. In short, all softwood lumber products-the bill requires a full page to list them all-will be affected, and a charge imposed shall be an amount equal to such percentage of the export price of the softwood lumber products, not exceeding 15 per cent thereof, as may be prescribed, up to a maximum of 15 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder exactly who will decide whether it's going to be less than 15 per cent, say 11, 12 or 8 per cent. I have tried to find out whether it was only the Government of Canada who was going to decide that, but when I examined the agreement-on this basis, I return to the issue of Canadian sovereignty, because the Minister herself has indicated that the clause concerning sovereignty in this bill was item No. 5 of the agreement. Well, dealing with the changes which could be made and included in Clause 5 of the bill, item 5b states, and I quote in English:
"Any such modifications in the export charge will be made by the Government of Canada. Calculation of the value of any replacement measures in relation to the export charge will be subject to further consultations and agreement between the two Governments." In fact, we will not be able to change the tax without the agreement of the U.S. Government. That is why I say that this Bill has really damaged the sovereignty of Canada.

When we consider the other aspects of this bill which deal with these changes, we realize that we still have to refer to the agreement-I do not know whether this is quite often the case with bills, my Parliamentary experience on this level being quite recent-but when we read in Paragraph 3 that in interpreting the schedule, recourse may be had to the Memorandum of Understanding between the Government of Canada and the Government of the United States, we understand that we must read both the bill and the Memorandum of Understanding and that no change in the tax could be made without the consent of the American Government.
Also, Mr. Speaker, the amounts collected by the Government of Canada would normally be shared between the provincial governments. Unfortunately, the time allotted to me will not permit me to deal with this issue, but it appears to me to be extremely important. I hope that before we complete the study of this bill, we will have at least a draft of the regulations, in order to know how they will be shared. But no matter the way they are shared, item 6 of the Memorandum states

that the amounts thus collected by the Government of Canada could not be used to provide the lumber industry in Canada with an advantage it did not enjoy before the signing of the agreement. In that context, I find its hard to understand how the Government can claim a victory by saying that the monies will be used to do reforestation work, because if reforestation work is done, that cannot be used to the benefit of the company and the company must establish a yearly balance sheet. And in that sense, this means that they will not be able to reach their stated goal, because this would be contrary to the agreement and if the agreement is not honoured, the American Government may terminate it within 30 days. And once it has been terminated because of Canada's failure to comply, as our leader pointed out in his speech earlier today, the U.S. President has the right to unilaterally impose a 10, 15 or 20 per cent tax he can determine himself. If this is not losing face as a country, Mr. Speaker, if we have not relinquished a major part of our sovereignty, I wonder what agreement, what situation could allow us to say otherwise.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in this debate as a Member from Quebec, after the Opposition Member who did not hesitate to call this Government and this Prime Minister naive and incompetent. It is very easy to pose as a swashbuckler and see the Canadian Government as a naive, incompetent and bad negotiator, to suggest it has been had, to consider this as a bad deal, a swindle, et cetera.
It is my view, Mr. Speaker, that there is a reason for the Bible to tell us about David and Goliath. It very seldom happens in real life unless God gets involved, and as God is both on Canada's and the United States' sides, God does not get involved in that matter, it very seldom happens that David overcomes Goliath. It is very seldom indeed that the smaller opponent will give a licking to the stronger one, the bigger one, the one with 25 times our population whose budgets and industrial base are world leaders, and the Opposition is asking that we act as swashbucklers, as winning Davids, as champions of Canadian nationalism, the stalwart supporters of interests that are now part of a global market.
In my view, it is sheer foolhardiness to go and get crucified in an arena where one is already sure of losing. There is but one intelligent possibility, that is to negotiate, and this is what we have been attempting to do, in line with the best interests of Canadians and the lumber industry.
If under previous Liberal Governments the Canadian dollar had been stronger than it was as a result of an economy that the Liberals had been literally massacring in Canada for many years, U.S. protectionism would have been less acute and we would not have been faced with the kind of difficult situations we are facing now.
Mr. Speaker, I am therefore going to put my question to the Hon. Member, and I would like to point out that the solution agreed upon with our American friends who are now experiencing internal problems as a result of which protectionism is king, that this solution is the one that is least damaging
to our economy and the one most in line with Canadian interests. Finally, and this is the question I would like to ask the previous speaker: Can our sovereignty of which he is so proud, and we share that pride with him, can this Canadian sovereignty extend beyond our borders?
I think we had a duty to negotiate the best possible arrangement in the circumstances. Would the Hon. Member agree with that?

Mr. Speaker, I've just spent all my time, twenty minutes of it, explaining why I did not agree, what I fail to understand, or rather, I do understand now what I did not understand before, and that is the entire state of mind that prevailed during these talks, and I don't know whether the Hon. Member for Charlevoix (Mr. Hamelin) is reflecting here what he heard in caucus from his Prime Minister, but if that is the state of mind prevailing within the Government, which consists in saying: the Americans are bigger than we are so we jump when they say jump, it is not surprising that we are where we are now. I always thought, and I still do, that we live in a country and on a continent where relations between citizens and between countries are governed by laws. It isn't the number of canons or the number of people that determine international relations. The Hon. Member for Charlevoix says the Americans are bigger and stronger. Americans live in a democratic country that tends to have respect for international agreements. In fact, in 1982-83, in an identical situation, a Government stood its ground and fought its case before the American courts, and Canada won a battle, the same battle this Government has refused to fight.
The Conservative Government simply went down on its knees as it did on the Foreign Investment Review Agency, with respect to books and other areas of our cultural industries, and is now doing with respect to pharmaceutical products. I am flabbergasted at the line of reasoning followed by the Hon. Member for Charlevoix, which appears to come straight from the Government benches and the confidential meetings they had, a line of reasoning that consists in saying that laws and international agreements don't count anymore, nowadays, every time someone who is bigger than we are says: move over, raise your taxes, lower them, remove that legislation, which means the Canadian Government will have to obey. In that case, Mr. Speaker, we are not living in a civilized world where the law forms the basis for relations, not just between individual citizens and between the citizen and his government, but also for all international activity. This would mean there would be an end to all that, and, Mr. Speaker, I think this truly reflects a defeatist attitude which certainly does not augur well for the rest of the talks, since it was this Government's decision as part of a comprehensive free trade agreement between our two countries.

speechtext:
I would like to put a question to my honourable friend.
January 19, 1987

Is the Hon. Member familiar with the Michelin case of 1972 wherein countervail was placed on Canadian tires by the United States because the Canadian Government saw fit to give Michelin a grant to establish in Nova Scotia which then became countervailable? To this day that decision causes problems with regard to regional disparity in this country. The Canadian Government of the day, which happened to be Liberal, did not fight that one. I cannot remember that Government talking about sovereignty then. I have other examples as well.
Does the Hon. Member remember that? Will he not admit that that was an intrusion in Canada by the United States and was, in fact, a far more severe intrusion on our sovereignty than is a negotiated settlement between two sovereign governments?

Mr. Speaker, I am completely flabbergasted by the question of the Hon. Member. It is unbelievable that he would compare a grant given to a foreign company which wanted to invest in Canada to the power of a province to establish the price of its natural resources. Is it possible to compare those two things and ask the question which he has asked? He is comparing the power of a province to sell its natural resources to a grant given by a government for an investment in a particular region of Canada.
I hope the Government will not settle the natural resources dispute based on that example. What happened in 1972 was a completely different case. If the Member is suggesting that a grant given by a government to a company must be considered as a possible countervailing duty by another country on the same footing as stumpage fees, a royalty on natural gas, or royalties on a mine, we should stop negotiating with the United States right now because we will lose our shirts.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate. This Bill and its implications will have a great effect on Canada's largest industry, something which I believe the House tends to forget from time to time. About one million Canadians are directly and indirectly employed in the forest sector. I want to deal with a little bit of the history of this matter because I think it involves an historic error of Government judgment which extends back to the time between 1983, when we were found innocent of the charge, and December 30, 1986, when this agreement was reached in Washington.
Before I do that, I will deal quickly with the final remarks made by the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney). She believes that one of the most important signs that this agreement is successful is the fact that stocks have gone up. I
Softwood Lumber Products Export Charge Act
believe the Minister is aware, as is everyone else in the House, that the reason they did that is that the incredible level of uncertainty surrounding this issue was gone. It certainly had nothing to do with the Ways and Means motion now before the House implementing a 15 per cent export tax.
The other Conservative Member who spoke demonstrated a level of naivete that I have not seen for some time in this House. He said that $400 million a year would now be spent on reforestation in B.C. He could not produce a single public statement or document indicating that that has been promised by anyone in British Columbia. With regard to the history of reforestation, the Social Credit Government of British Columbia has the worst track record of any government in the history of Canada. We have "not satisfactorily restocked" lands larger than Prince Edward Island. These lands have never been replanted by the Government or the companies which logged them.
To indicate to British Columbians and other Canadians that the $600 million collected under the export tax is in any way, shape, or form going to be going into reforestation, retraining, or market or plant diversification, is to give false hope which I do not think government or opposition Members should give to people who work in the woods, whether they are buckers, fallers, skidder operators or work in planer mills or sawmills or anything else. I think this debate should be far more frank. It is for that reason that I will discuss for a few moments the history of this issue.
As a Parliament and a country we should have fought much more vigorously. I think we could have won. I believe that if the academics, historians, and legal scholars took a close look at this issue they would realize how we should have fought this battle. There are Hon. Members here during the debate this evening who were at the meeting with me in Washington, in other areas of the United States and in Vancouver where it became clear that the protectionist fervour, coming particularly from members of the Congress and Senate from producing states, was starting to move the administration. What we should have done almost two years ago was to have fanned out trade consulates throughout the United States in selected states and cities and got accurate information out to American consumers about the effects of the proposals of the U.S. coalition on U.S. consumers. We managed through our U.S. Embassy to get to a few people and a few newspapers. There were a few editorials written. However, the U.S. consumers are still in the dark. What has happened is one of the most complex situations of price fixing of which I am aware, although I have only been here seven-odd years.
Let us get a few things clear on the record. Canadian SPF, spruce pine fir, is preferentially purchased in the United States by contractors and homebuilders. They pay a higher price. They have always paid a higher price. They know it is a better quality wood for studs, joists, rafters and for general basic construction. One should look at the tracking of the exchange

January 19, 1987
Softwood Lumber Products Export Charge Act
rate. The argument should have been about the exchange rate. As we took more market share in the United States, it tracked perfectly day by day, week by week, month by month, the exchange differential between Canada and the United States. We picked up that market, certainly a big chunk of it from B.C. producers, some of it from other areas of the country, but we tracked into that market because the wood is preferentially purchased.
As the housing markets went up, we picked up more of that market because of the exchange rate. So a group of producers in the United States got together and asked: "How are we going to get our prices up? We can't price fix in the United States. We can't even talk about it because of anti-trust legislation in the United States". I have talked to a lot of Canadian producers about what Canada could have and should have done in dealing with this issue. However, the Americans got to Washington and from 1983 onward a lot of money was spent and they were very careful about who they were moving, people such as Senator Mattingly, Senator Baucus, and Senator Packwood. They knew how to get to Sam Gibbons. They knew all the key players they had to get moving in terms of the U.S. administration.
Finally, we had the most preposterous letter I have ever seen, the May 8, 1986 famed "Dear Bob" letter from President Reagan which I will read later into the record. They were very well organized. They wanted a larger market share. We retooled our mills on time in British Columbia, in Alberta, in Saskatchewan, to a small extent in Manitoba, and in Ontario, Quebec and the Maritimes. We spent the money as a country, as corporations. We have much more highly productive workers. We had a much better industry and we have better wood. The Americans asked: "How do we get more southern yellow pine on to the market? How do we get these antiquated mills running again? How do we get people in the United States to buy this crappy wood again?" They asked how they could get American consumers to pay $1,000 to $4,000 more per unit. American consumers should be kicking those Senators and members of the Congress around the block for this form of price fixing. Instead, we are having a debate which makes me as a Canadian feel ill. We know if one takes $600 million out of an industry which only made $600 million last year, that industry will be in trouble.
I will refer to page 5 of the most recent Hay-Roe's and read what he feels is likely to happen in the cyclical downturn in terms of interest rates and the slowdown in the U.S. housing market. This is from the November-December issue of Hay-Roe's-.
The problem Canada faces, then, is that a rise in interest rates will not only generate a downturn in the lumber market, but will also increase the sawmillers' interest costs. Such a squeeze might have been bearable without a tariff to hurdle, but that 15 per cent off the top could be the undoing of the weaker or higher-cost Canadian companies.
For next year, a trend-line (3 per cent) increase in costs, coupled with the cost of the tariff, would shrink gross profits from $50 to $20 (Canadian dollars) per thousand board feet; and that is the result before allowing for any cyclical weakness in the market.
If we then knock off a "normal" cyclical price decline-which should be expected in 1988 or 1989-the full horror of the situation is evident. A typical cyclical decline since World War II has been about a 20 per cent drop, using annual average prices. Applying that percentage to our hoped-for 1987 average price implies a drop of more than $50 Canadian (almost $40 U.S.).
This would run our aggregate gross margin for the Canadian industry about $30 into the hole-much worse than the losses seen even in 1982-and that assumes no further increase in unit costs.

Canadian industry.
Let us go back, Mr. Speaker, to that window of opportunity. We heard when we were in Washington that we should be doing this. We brought that message back to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark). We brought it to the then Minister for International Trade. Not a thin dime was put forward. However, today we find out that the Minister for International Trade wants to spend $12 million, after the fact, on a salvage operation at least in relation to the softwood issue. It had the window of opportunity to get to U.S. consumers, who would in turn get to U.S. legislators to have them back off, and I do not know why Cabinet did not do it. I know it received the message because it came from us, the all-member committee which went to the United States a number of times. I discussed it directly with some of the Ministers who were involved but they did not carry it any further. That real opportunity was gone and now we are into all of what I consider to be somewhat false arguments which are going on in the House today. We know in 1983 we won the case before the same tribunal, before the International Trade Commission. Everyone then started saying it was double jeopardy to be tried again and we will win it again. So the industry put $10 million in its basket and went down and fought it in Washington. It lobbied. It had lawyers. It did this and that and held out the hope to Canadian workers and companies that we would simply win.
I believe many Hon. Members of the House honestly thought we were going to win. Then things started to come unwound partly in relation to a statement made this fall by the Minister of Forests in British Columbia. That was followed by the Premier of British Columbia, Mr. Vander Zalm, when he said the stumpage policies were going to have to be reviewed and so on. That was the first political admission that the forest industry in British Columbia was being subsidized. The Americans immediately picked up that statement and ran with it in the United States. There were three blinks by Mr. Vander Zalm and every worker in the Canadian forest industry-and it was certainly well known in the corporate boardrooms- knew that the loose lips of Vander Zalm were the first thing which really started getting us into trouble.
The famed three blinks were the political admission of the subsidy, then it was said they were going to go it alone to Washington and then it was said that the deal had been struck which, of course, was totally erroneous. The Premier had heard someone said something on television and called a press conference, which was ridiculous. Adding to that was the problem created by the Minister for International Trade in going to Washington, and being pushed around by the Premier
January 19, 1987

of British Columbia and perhaps by some other forces, she said: "We are making this once only final offer of 10 per cent. That is it. Take it or leave it". This is after we had made arguments. I was there along with the Hon. Member for Cariboo-Chilcotin (Mr. Greenaway) and other Members of the House and we told the Americans they were wrong. We told them about double jeopardy, about double counting. We told them all of the things which were wrong with their arguments. They knew we were right.
I know the reason Mr. Vander Zalm wants this export tax. He will never convert this to stumpage increases. He will never do that because there is no incentive for him to do so. He can take this cash and pave roads with it or whatever he bloody well pleases. It will never go into reforestation. I think it unfair and erroneous for Hon. Members to stand in this House and say this is a windfall, that stocks are going up, that it means reforestation programs and no one will lose their jobs. They should read Mike MacEachern. He says 4,700 jobs will be lost. Charlie Widman, not the most accurate guy in the world, says somewhere in the neighbourhood of 40 sawmills will close and
17,000	jobs will be lost.
What we do know is this tax will take away $600 million which could be going back into the industry. It is going to take that money and put it into provincial hands and it will be damn difficult to make any kind of new agreement or arrangement which the Americans will accept because there is no incentive for the Canadians to come forward with a legitimate proposal the Americans would buy, nor is there any serious likelihood, with the variation there is in stumpage in Canada at $10 a thousand in British Columbia, $36 a thousand in Ontario, $40 in Quebec and far higher than that in New Brunswick. With those kinds of ratios what incentive is there for British Columbia, the largest producer to do that? British Columbia will get a larger market share within Canada and in relation to the gross size of the market in the United States as well. Mr. Speaker, I need at least an hour to finish my remarks. I have not even dealt with my notes yet.
I would now like to deal with some of the arguments I heard made in this place by members of the Government and by others. One argument was that we could have won at the ITC or in the courts. The reason given for not going through with that process is that there would have been years of battle. That is quite true. To have carried on the fight at great length in terms of the U.S. court system, having waited beyond December 30 when the petition could not be withdrawn, would have involved a very lengthy process. There is no doubt about that.
Let me now deal with the real issue which is that if we are all standing together on the concept that Canada is a sovereign nation, then we should have fought this matter all the way through. There have been a great many erroneous statements made about what the positions of different people are. We should have fought the conservatives in the United States. The Government decided not to do that, and we will let that be.

Then there was the Department of Commerce process to be considered. It goes through a process of double addition. All of us who are members of the Forestry Committee have been through that process. The highest figure which it could have come up with, using its own figures, would have been a 7 per cent countervail. We know that. We know that 15 per cent is illegal. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has said that, and so have I. A great many people have said that. It was an illegal countervail duty. It was an administrative decision made for political reasons.
How can that type of politics be dealt with? I do not think our Government ever sat down to try to address the issue. This matter involves the biggest industry in Canada. Softwood lumber accounts for the largest source of balance of trade. Yet what did the Government do? It let the first window close and when the second one came along, an illegal countervail presented itself. The Minister stood up twice in the House and said: "We will fight this all the way". She said: "We will do everything we can". I think at that point in time we should have really mobilized.
What was going on in the United States? More disinformation and more misinformation. Reporters on U.S. television networks were saying that the reason wood prices were going to increase in the United States was because of Canada. I raised this issue here in the House. A television station in Florida, and other news broadcasters, have said that the whole issue regarding softwood lumber was created by Canada.
The Americans got away with misinformation, illegal processes and administrative decisions. It is all very well for the Minister to get up and say that we had to get the precedent off the books. The fact of the matter is that a far worse precedent is now on the books. The Americans blackmailed us to begin with. They had a powerful lobby which set representatives to their politicians. The politicians went to the Department of Commerce and to the ITC. They came up with an illegal administrative decision and then said: "Okay, Mr. Prime Minister, you take the gun. We are going to nail you for 15 per cent. Hold it to your head and shoot yourself. We will not put the 15 per cent. You go ahead and shoot yourself'. So we sent some guys down to Washington. The Minister for International Trade was off on the other side of the planet. These guys went down and negotiated what they could. But they did not have much to deal with. What were they to do? They wrote a few things down. There was a ways and means motion and we heard them say: "People will not be hurt too much".
The fact of the matter is that when I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) here in the House, he would not offer any kind of guarantee that there will be federal assistance for those workers or those companies which will be hurt by this export tax. We know who they will be. Through the Forestry Committee we have been asking for months to obtain a list of those companies which are most likely to be knocked out first. We know who they are. They are small companies working in high-cost timber. They are fairly far from the

market or they are already paying a higher royalty than that paid in other areas of the country. We already know who they are. Those people are frightened. Those workers are frightened because they go to work and the company says: "We cannot have a union here anymore because we have this 15 per cent tax so let us get rid of that collective agreement. You are now being paid $8 an hour. We will have to shave it down to $5 in order to deal with this export tax. We have to do this to stay in the market". That type of dialogue has already started. The people are frightened. We know that some of these mills are only marginally competitive now. A great many of them have been swimming in red ink for years.
Scare tactics!

Scare tactics? Members of the Government have stood in their places and made totally erroneous statements with respect to S400 million per year in B.C. going for reforestation. That is absolutely and totally false. The Hon. Member who made that statement could not direct Members of the House to a single public statement or document that has ever come out in that regard. Talk about erroneous bafflegab! I would use much stronger language to describe it if I were not in the House; but you know I will not, Mr. Speaker.
The Minister has travelled around the country and said: "Members of the NDP and the Liberals say that the money should all go to the United States". Who does the Government think it will con with that type of statement? A six-year-old child could tell us that it is better for the $600 million to stay in Canada than to go to the United States. That is not the argument. There has been blatant government incompetence and backing-down to the bully tactics of the United States. That is what is at issue here. We should have fought as a country. They do not understand any of those things, but they understand that this is merely the latest in a series of capitulations by a Government that claims to speak for Canada. That they understand very well.
Is it not amusing that on Wednesday of this week, in 48-hours' time, the Vice-President of the United States with a cabinet secretary in tow will arrive in Canada? The VicePresident did not come to Canada in a panic when Canadians were screaming about the impact of the cedar shakes and shingles issue. There was no sign of a U.S. presidential aircraft touching down in Ottawa. The Vice-President did not arrive in Canada when we screamed like hell about the imposition of American ice-breakers in Canadian Arctic waters. There was no sign of an American presidential aircraft then. He did not arrive when duties were imposed on pork and fish. He did not even come when we screamed like hell when the softwood lumber deal was signed. But, by God, just one week after the branch plant, the subsidiary of the Republican Party in Canada which is the Tory Party goes to third in the polls and the cursed, frightening socialists go to second, the Vice President with a cabinet secretary in tow will arrive.
Why will he arrive? Is it because he wants to discuss trade issues? Is it because he is concerned that Canadians have been speaking with one angry voice about the treatment we have received at the hands of an insensitive American administration? No, he is arriving because it is the American mentality that when the branch plant is in trouble, the head office goes to visit. When the Canadian subsidiary is not producing up to scratch, the head office goes to see it. Now that the branch plant, the Canadian subsidiary of the American Republican Party, the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada, is in trouble, the Vice-President and a cabinet secretary are riding
in on the big silver wings of the American presidential emblem in an attempt to bail out a Prime Minister who has panicked, pushed the direct line to Washington and said: "Come bail me out". I do not know how successful that is going to be.
I was in Washington a week ago. I want to tell Hon. Members that as much as we are totally absorbed and obsessed, and rightly so, with events which have occurred over the last year, events which have crystallized in this ridiculous Bill through the imposition of an American Government's will on a sovereign Canadian state, in Washington, well, they are not really interested. They hardly know there is an issue here. It is an incredibly frightening realization to see on the front page of every single newspaper in Washington and on every American television network reports about a potential trade war between the U.S. and the EEC. What is at stake? The Americans might impose $250 million in duties on gin and pasta imported from the EEC. That was a front page story. Meanwhile the $500 million in duties imposed on softwood lumber was nowhere to be found. Why would a $250 million tariff threatened against the EEC dominate the imagination of Americans and a $500 million tariff imposed on a Canadian product be studiously ignored? Let me tell you why. Without getting into who is right and who is wrong in that dispute, the EEC has responded to the American threat by telling the Americans that they run the risk of a full-scale trade war if that $250 million tariff is imposed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: Are you suggesting we get into a trade war?
I am suggesting no one should get into a trade war but I am suggesting that we do not get down on bended knee-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade

-like some supplicating protectorate-

That is true!

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: You know all about wind.

The difference is that the EEC has said to the Americans that kind of imposition will not be accepted by them. In Canada we have quietly knuckled under and agreed to negotiate, to compromise, to try and find some face-saving
January 19, 1987

gesture which allows the Canadian Government to claim a measure of victory and at the same time meeting precisely the terms and conditions of its masters in Washington.

You must be embarrassed as a Government to be put in such a-
Oh, come on.

A former Member of the House, Mr. Jean Chretien-
Oh, oh!
-used to tell a story-

What did he tell Turner?
Perhaps that is a lesson for the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: He got hit by an iceberg.

Softwood Lumber Products Export Charge Act
rather than cross the bridge on its knees. The Government has set a precedent in this natural resource pricing which will allow the American Government to demand similar treatment in other areas, whether it be pulp and paper, newsprint, agricultural products, or any other specialized field. The Government has entered into an agreement that establishes a precedent which is extremely dangerous for Canada.
We heard the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) talk about the sovereignty clause in the agreement. We heard her contend that the letter written by Mr. Baldrige and Mr. Yeutter to Mr. Dennison of the American lumber industry is nothing but a political side-show. I want to tell Members that when I was in Washington last week with my colleague from Winnipeg we met with Mr. Alan Woods, the senior American administration-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade

We have already talked about little crackys. If that noisy big cracky will hold his tongue for a moment, I will continue with my speech.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: Bugger all.

The Member opposite, a Parliamentary Secretary, says it means bugger all. Is the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) about to tell the Vice-President of the U.S. on Wednesday that the American administration interpretation means bugger all?

speechtext: Order, please. The Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) on a point of order.
