speechtext: I will check it out and I will be able to rule on it tomorrow. The time for the Hon. Member's speech has expired. I will give him an extra three minutes and we will then move on to questions and comments.

Mr. Speaker, I will obviously respect the ruling of the Chair. With respect to the terminology I used, I am just a fellow from Newfoundland. We do not use that kind of terminology down there. The Progressive Conservative Member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid) used the term and I was merely repeating it for the benefit of his colleague who objects to it. I suggest he have a private tete-a-tete with the Hon. Member about his language if he does not like it. I am nothing but an echo, and from time to time a foolish echo, of the insensitive and foolish comments I hear across the way while I am speaking.
It is my belief that the agreement which has been signed between the United States and Canada on the lumber accord is such a bad agreement in terms of its impact on Canadian sovereignty and such a bad agreement in terms of the legal precedent which it sets with respect to the American ability to set prices for our natural resources, that Canada would be better off if it moved to invoke Article 9 of the agreement. That is the article which allows us to terminate the agreement within 30 days. If that means that at that point we have to run the risk of American retaliation, that we have to find enough backbone and resolve to stand up and be a sovereign, independent, mature nation rather than a loose protectorate of
the United States, then so be it. Let us stand up and be counted.
If this nation, in the interest of ensuring that the Prime Minister is able to keep alive the free trade talks which he has committed so much political capital to, has to continue to concede to the Americans and appease them on every single irritant they raise, be it generic drugs, cedar shakes and shingles, lumber, fish, pork, or Arctic sovereignty, the only difference between us and Puerto Rico would be that Puerto Rico is formally a U.S. protectorate and Canada would be a protectorate posturing as a nation. We in this Party will not see that day arrive without a hell of a lot of noise and debate.

Mr. Speaker, I have a short question for the Hon. Member after his excellent presentation. On January 3, 1987, the Canadian Press made the following statement:
Historians, economists and legal scholars give the Mulroney government a failing grade on its handling of the softwood lumber talks with the United States.
They say the government has jeopardized Canada's sovereignty by caving in to American demands to impose a 15-per-cent tax on lumber exports south of the border.
And they say there is no precedent in Canadian history for a deal that gives Washington a voice in how Canada manages its lumber industry.
Maxwell Cohen, one of Canada's foremost experts on international law, said Friday that the lumber deal is a dangerous precedent that threatens Canadian sovereignty.
"It is a strange procedure to allow someone to monitor our own stuff," said Cohen, who was a judge on the International Court of Justice in the Gulf of Maine dispute with the U.S. and a former Canadian chairman of the International Joint Commission.
Does the Hon. Member support the suggestion in this Canadian Press report that this is in fact a very serious erosion of Canadian sovereignty, particularly in the softwood industry?

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Hon. Member for his very tough and penetrating question. I will attempt to answer it. There is no doubt that the agreement which has been signed by the Government of Canada, taken on its own merit, is an erosion of sovereignty. This agreement follows a series of other matters which were so-called negotiated between our two nations. We retaliated against the tariff on cedar shakes by putting a tariff on teabags and American books. The Americans applied a tariff to salt fish products in Atlantic Canada. Since only Atlantic Canada was affected, the Government of Canada went to sleep on it. It did not matter.
The American administration sailed an ice-breaker through Arctic waters and, rather than spending its time protesting strongly, making a claim of Canadian sovereignty, or demanding that such an exercise never occur again, the Canadian Government tried to explain that it did not know until after the fact that Americans had moved into our sovereign waters. The Americans have prodded a few times. They sent a ship racing through our sovereign waters and we did nothing. They imposed a 35 per cent tariff on shakes and shingles and we retaliated on teabags. The Americans are not stupid. After a while they begin to learn something. If you poke an animal
January 19, 1987

that is cornered and it only whimpers, it is time to get rough. The Americans got rough. The most humiliating thing about this agreement is not that we whimpered, but that we actually pretended we had won something great.
I grew up on American Air Force bases. My father was employed with the American Air Force for 30 years. Americans are as good a people as you will find anywhere in the world. However, I know that you have a good relationship with anyone when there is mutual respect across the fence. The Americans have no respect for the vacillating Tory administration which they see across the fence.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Member for Kamloops- Shuswap (Mr. Riis) quoted former Judge Cohen. I hope the Member realizes that Professor Cohen is strongly supportive of the bilateral initiative.
I have a two-part question for the Member. What would his Party have done with respect to softwood lumber? Would it have allowed the $600 million to go out of the country? Does it not feel that stumpage fees should be raised in British Columbia and other provinces? Second, bearing in mind that about 2.5 million Canadian citizens depend upon the U.S. market for their livelihood, what is the policy of the Member's Party with respect to the bilateral negotiations with the United States?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to believe that any administration, theoretically even Conservative, although that is doubtful, that demonstrated some resolve, that demonstrated that it took the notion of nationhood seriously, that demonstrated that it took the notion of sovereignty seriously, would not have been confronted with an American administration prepared to make a 360 degree turn from the ruling it made in 1983 to the completely opposite ruling it made in 1986.
What we saw was not an exercise in trade law, as the Hon. Member knows. We saw an exercise in the United States of the lowest form of politics. No commerce department can justify doing a complete flip-flop on the basis of trade law. That could only occur in the face of political heat at home and a consideration by the administration that this kind of action could be taken against Canada because Canada had neither the backbone nor the resolve to respond in a proper way. We would quite likely not have been faced with this problem. If we were, we would not have given up our remedies under countervail law or under international law.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, why does the Hon. Member continue to believe in and support the side letter written by the Americans which has nothing to do with the agreement? Those who have negotiated and those who are giving legal advice to the Canadian Government say that that letter is not the agreement. The agreement is the one which was signed. Their interpretation is entirely different. Why does the Member believe the Americans rather than the Canadians? Why does he continue to insist on that?
Adjournment Debate

Mr. Speaker, this is almost amusing. It is not a matter of whether or not I believe the Americans. The fact is that under the agreement which Canada has signed with the United States, Canada has no method of appeal. We have no remedies. We signed them away.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: You do have remedies.

No, we do not. The Americans have Section 301 of the American Trade Law which is a huge hammer with which they intend, when necessary, to hit us. It does not matter whether I choose to believe the Americans or the Canadians because the Americans in this agreement are the only ones with the clout under the agreement to hammer our side into submission. The Americans have said publicly to the press and to the media through their ambassador that this is their interpretation of the agreement. If we can find no common ground on what the agreement means, then the Parliamentary Secretary is really admitting we do not have an agreement.

subtopic: CANADIAN HUMAN RIGHTS COMMISSION-RESIGNATION OF ANTONIO ARCANGEL FROM HUMAN RIGHTS TRIBUNAL
CANADIAN HUMAN RIGHTS COMMISSION-RESIGNATION OF ANTONIO ARCANGEL FROM HUMAN RIGHTS TRIBUNAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I apologize for my croaky voice this evening. I seem to have caught the flu bug or whatever it is that is going around. The appointment of Antonio Arcangel to the Canadian Human Rights Tribunal and his subsequent resignation was the subject matter of my question in the House to the Hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) back in November. It is a question which raises once again a much wider issue. It raises a question which will not go away. That is, the question of the whole appointments process, regardless of the facts in the Antonio Arcangel case and regardless of whether one thinks it is a good appointment or a bad appointment, and there are just as many people who think it was a good appointment as think it was a bad one. As you, Mr. Speaker, and other Members of Parliament may know, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has received many letters in support of that appointment. However, regardless of whether it was a good or bad appointment, there is a larger issue which transcends that appointment, or any others, and that is the question of the actual appointment process itself.
You will remember, Mr. Speaker, when this issue was first raised. It was raised originally in the election campaign of 1984 during the famous debate which many people think turned the whole election around. The now Leader of the
2414

January 19, 1987
Adjournment Debate
Opposition (Mr. Turner), the then Prime Minister, was asked by a questioner whether or not he was required to make certain appointments which were recommended to him by the former Prime Minister, the Right Hon. Pierre Elliott Trudeau. He said: "But I had no choice". The now Prime Minister responded saying: "But you did have a choice", and that was a very turning point in the election campaign. As a result of that statement and that exchange, the Canadian people came to feel, as I firmly believe, that there was a promise made. It was not an express promise but an implied promise that there would be changes in the whole process of appointments.
After the massive election of our majority Government there were apparently some changes. There were appointments made of New Democratic adherents and Liberal adherents to various positions both in the beginning and subsequently. However, as time went on the only thing which appeared in the press time after time was the appointment of people who were adherents of the Progressive Conservative Party. As a result of that the public began to feel that nothing had changed, that all was the same as it was before.
As you and I know, Mr. Speaker, the public came to believe that the people appointed were all affiliated with the Progressive Conservative Party, many friends of the Prime Minister. They came to believe that the process of appointments was not as open as they thought it was going to be. They came to believe that the people being appointed were not the best qualified regardless of whether or not they were well qualified. They began to feel let down and that feeling reinforced the feeling of non-confidence in the Government they had elected.
You and I may very well feel, Mr. Speaker, that there is no reason for Canadians to feel let down because the former Government did the same thing and provincial Governments, whether Liberal or New Democratic, are doing exactly the same thing. However, the public felt there was going to be a change and that change did not occur. They saw the same thing happening. In fact, in September of 1985 the Prime Minister announced a change. He announced that there would be a process of parliamentary review of appointments.
What happened as a result of that parliamentary review process? We had cases such as the Antonio Arcangel case. So while the review process by committee may be a good one, and one which I support whole-heartedly, it is not the entire answer. We need a new type of appointment process, one which I wish to suggest to Hon. Members of the House and to the public tonight.
First, what we need is a public appointments office, one that is not hidden away in the Prime Minister's office or in the office of the Privy Council. It must be one that is open to the public so that the public can see what is going on.
Second, at the beginning of each year we need to place an ad in all daily newspapers and all ethnic newspapers across the country stating that we will be making some appointments this
year to boards and agencies and if anyone is interested then let us know. Then, when Members of the public respond, what we should do is write back to them providing a list of the appointments we will be making and ask them to let us know in which ones they are interested. When they write back to us, we should send them another letter with application forms and job descriptions for particular positions. That is the sort of process which should be taking place.
When the applications are returned, we should review them and make a short list of the best possible candidates regardless of all other circumstances. The choice should then be reviewed by the committee process which is in place and then the appointments should be made.
I do not expect the Parliamentary Secretary to announce that form of appointment process tonight. However, I would like him to take my suggestion to the Prime Minister and to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) and return with an answer for me later on.

subtopic: STATUS OF WOMEN-FUNDING OF WOMEN'S ORGANIZATIONS
STATUS OF WOMEN-FUNDING OF WOMEN'S ORGANIZATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 12 of last year I posed a question to the Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie) to which I received what I consider to be an unsatisfactory answer. The question concerned what I perceived to be a bias in his Department in terms of the funding of women's programs. I might add that same perception is shared by a number of my colleagues in the House, as well as a large number of people in my riding and across Canada.
The question is not whether Government should be funding the many specific worth-while women's projects, but rather whether Government should be supplying sustaining funds to lobby groups. It is my belief that Government should not be funding any lobby group with taxpayers' dollars. Certainly some of the groups applying for and receiving funds specifically under the women's program are just that. However, if Government is going to fund such groups, then it should be done fairly and with balance.
Unfortunately, since I raised the issue the Minister has seen fit to deny funding to one group which has strong views on many women's issues. At the same time, he is maintaining funding to another group that also has strong views, but views that are quite different from the group that was denied funding.
The objective of the women's program of the Secretary of State is to support the full participation of women in all aspects-Mr. Speaker, I wish to repeat that-in all aspects of Canadian society, and to increase the capability of women's organizations and groups working to improve the status of women. In addition, it is also intended to promote increased understanding and action on women's issues among women and the general public in the form of advocacy and information exchange. I fully support that objective. But I do not agree with the interpretation being put on it by the Department or by the Minister.
As I look around the House, I regret that it appears there is no one here to respond on behalf of the Minister. It is a slight to which I as an individual Member have to take exception. Be that as it may, I wish to carry on with my presentation.
In response to my question in the House, the Minister responded: "The process we use at the Department of Secretary of State for assessment of all applications is a just and fair one, and I expect to continue that process". How can a process be just and fair when one group is not allowed the opportunity to participate in that process? The refusal by the Department to send application forms to any group under any program is inexcusable.
I believe that we have a very unjust and unfair process when bureaucrats, who do not share the same philosophy on issues as a significant group of the public, have the power to deny that group access to the process. I was pleased to see in the
Adjournment Debate
Minister's announcement last Thursday that he has acknowledged the shoddy treatment that was accorded to some women's groups in their application for funds. That does not excuse the Department for what has gone on prior to him being appointed Minister. I believe that there are a significant number of women in this country, who, while wanting equality in all areas, have some strong convictions on such issues as child rearing, family role models, sexual orientation and pornography, to name but a few. The promotion of those ideals does not qualify for funding at the present time under the present criteria.
On the other hand, another group receiving approval for funding has policies supporting positions such as withdrawing Canada from NATO and NORAD, declaring Canada a nuclear-free zone, involving all women in the struggle for lesbian rights, and state-run and financed universal day care, again to name but a few.
I believe that I could identify the group which reflects the opinion of a large segment of the population in my riding, and of a great number of other ridings across this country, not only women, but men as well, and it would not be the latter group which would receive that approval.
I apologize for nobody being here to respond on behalf of the Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie).

speakeroldname: Mr. Vincent Della Noce (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport); Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism)
subtopic: STATUS OF WOMEN-FUNDING OF WOMEN'S ORGANIZATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was on the other side of the House, but I was listening to my hon. friend.
The Hon. Member for Brampton-Middlesex (Mr. Fraleigh) asked a question of the Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie) last December 12 about funding to women's groups by his Department's women's programs. I should now like to tell the House what are the Government's objectives.
The three main objectives the federal Government is pursuing on behalf of women are: economic equality, social justice, and access and participation.
Through economic equality we are trying to ensure that women are economically secure and benefit equally from their contribution to Canadian society. This is a primary objective when one thinks that today 64 per cent of women aged 20 years to 64 years are in the labour force and that they continue to be clustered in low-income occupations. Also, women make up 43 per cent of the total labour force.
The second objective, that of social justice, took on new importance on April 17, 1985 when Article 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms came into force. This

January 19, 1987
Adjournment Debate
important article deals with equality. In addition to the rulings which courts will apply over the next few years, the objective takes in, among other things, the formulation of new laws, violence directed toward women, pornography, and the stereotyping of women by the media.
The third main objective covers access and participation. It refers to equitable social and economic access, the participation of women in decision-making processes, and the battle against attitudinal discrimination when they occupy nontraditional posts.
There are two types of assistance provided by the women's program of the Department of the Secretary of State- operational funding and project funding. The first is used to promote the ongoing existence of national and regional women's organizations capable of taking co-ordinated action on issues of concern to women. Project funding is given in support of short-term projects linked to current objectives of the Government.
In 1985-86 the program funded more than 500 projects and the administration of 129 organizations. In all these cases, their objective was to remove obstacles to the equality of women in society. You can well understand, Mr. Speaker, that the women's program of the Department of the Secretary of State cannot aid all women's groups. It has to follow the priorities the Government has set for itself.
All requests received by the women's program are examined by criteria, including how a particular project will help women reach equality and the capacity of the requesting group to handle its respective project. As the Secretary of State said himself in the House on December 12, all requests are handled in the same manner-justly and equally.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what we have just seen is not "The decline of the American Empire", but "The decline of the Conservative Government". I can understand why the Conservative Member is disappointed with such a reply. I do not blame the Parliamentary Secretary, but this shows the mess and disorganization within this Conservative Government. In fact, the Secretary's reply was entirely beside the point, and nobody was prepared to reply. This is an insult made to a Member which I will defend, even if he is from the Progressive Conservative Party. I dare hope that I will obtain from the Parliamentary Secretary a better reply to the question I had directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration concerning the cuts in unemployment insurance benefits to 35,000 early retirees in Canada, including 11,000 in the Province of Quebec. Everybody will recall that, in 1985, any worker who had contributed to a pension scheme through employee-employer
deductions and who lost his job could continue to collect full unemployment insurance benefits while looking for another job. Any person who had accepted to take early retirement to surrender his permanent job to a younger person and seek a second career could continue to collect full unemployment insurance benefits while seeking another job, even while collecting pension benefits for which he or she had contributed through employee-employer deductions for 25, 30 or 35 years of his or her life.
Everybody knows that, unfortunately, the Mulroney Cabinet decided on December 20, 1985, that beginning on January 5, 1986, the Unemployment Insurance Commission would take into account, while computing benefits, all incomes from a private employer-employee pension plan.
All groups throughout Canada got organized, even the Conservative Members, the Liberal Opposition, the New Democratic Party, all people were opposed to this decision. The then Minister and her colleague the Minister of Employment and Immigration said they would heed the Forget Commission recommendation as to whether this regulation ought to be changed.
Mr. Forget released his report on December 3 and his recommendation 26 concerning early retirees was quite clear. With respect to the inclusion of private pension plan benefits in calculating unemployment insurance, recommendation 26 stated clearly that the Government must retroactively rescind this measure, and if in future there should be another such measure concerning pension benefits and unemployment insurance he recommended that it be announced by the Government three years in advance because it is very important that someone who has worked all his life and planned for retirement not be forced to cope with a Government which changes the rules of the game.
On December 5 the Minister of Employment and Immigration said in this House that as a result of the Forget Commission recommendations he would make changes and forthwith direct the Unemployment Insurance Commission to launch a review process designed to reimburse the 35,000 early retirees whose unemployment insurance benefits had been cut off.
Mr. Speaker, nothing has been done to this day. The only action taken was the one I witnessed last week in the Montreal region where 1,000 early retirees who were denied these benefits attended a meeting convened by Quebec City ARSAC representatives. On Thursday this week these people will be in the Saguenay region, in the riding of the Minister of Employment and Immigration, and they have met with residents of Baie-Comeau and the Quebec City region. The only action came from the people themselves who prepared their own reimbursement request form to ensure that the Government would reimburse retroactively all the retirees who have been unfairly penalized.
I trust that the Parliamentary Secretary-and I know that, not only Friday, but also today, at the community centre of my
January 19, 1987

constituency, 300 people from Greater Montreal came, as well as people from the Laval area because they wanted justice.
Unfortunately, in this matter as in many others, the Government is dragging its feet. Yet, we can recall how quickly the Conservative Government passed legislation to reimburse $1 billion to people who had $60,000 deposits in Western banks. In this case, the people involved are workers throughout the country who, for 35 or 25 years, accepted lower wage increases to put away some money in a pension plan each month, but now, all their efforts are being penalized.
Mr. Speaker, I trust that the Parliamentary Secretary will give us a more satisfactory answer than the one he must have had from the Department of the Secretary of State and that he will give us a clear and specific answer about when the Government intends to reimburse these people and find a method to determine the amount of their reimbursement, and second, when the Minister will table a bill to extend eligibility not only to 1985 retirees, but also to 1986 and all future retirees so that, from now on, unemployment insurance premiums will be fully and completely reimbursed to all individuals, whatever their private pension income, since the Government does not make any deduction in the case of an RRSP.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-(A) REQUEST FOR REIMBURSEMENT OF CONTRIBUTIONS TO EARLY RETIREES (B) REQUEST THAT MINISTER MEET REPRESENTATIVES OF INTERESTED PARTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in turn, I would like to answer on behalf of the Minister of Employment and Immigration and expand on the question the Hon. Member put in the House on October 31, 1986. I am aware of the abiding interest of the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) in the matter, but unfortunately, I do not have as much time as he did and I will therefore try to be very brief and expeditious. This is our only chance to respond, and I hope the Hon. Member doesn't think I am going to indicate any changes in regulations previously announced by the Minister.
On December 5, 1986, the Minister announced changes in the unemploymenty insurance regulations concerning pension income. These changes will allow workers who take another job after retirement and keep that job long enough to become eligible for unemployment insurance benefits to receive such
Adjournment Debate
benefits without having the amount of their previous pension income subtracted from their benefits.
On November 8, 1984, as my hon. friend said, the Minister of Finance, announced in his agenda for economic renewal the Government's intention to consider pension income as remuneration for the purposes of establishing unemployment insurance benefits. The principle that continues to guide us today is that retired persons should not consider unemployment insurance as an additional source of income. The objective of the Unemployment Insurance Fund is to provide a replacement income to people temporarily out of work. The major policy change announced in November 1984 did not make a clear distinction between those retiring for good and those retiring to start a new career. The best example is provided by military personnel and RCMP officers who must take early retirement. The changes announced December 5 of last year will mean a fair and equitable treatment for this group of people who continue to be part of the labour force. Workers who have started a new career, where they must contribute to unemployment insurance, and subsequently lose their job will be entitled to full unemployment insurance benefits based on their previous pension income.
Besides, as mentioned by my colleague, some retirees who were in receipt of benefits as of January 5, 1986, when the former policy came into effect, lost their rights to benefits and will not regain them if they have left the job market. Some of these people argue that they based their decision to retire on erroneous information provided to them from federal government sources. In order to clear this matter, the Employment and Immigration Commission will review all such cases and reinstitute the right to benefits if the allegations are proven. The review will be done according to the normal procedures for claim settlement and we should note that the Government has always acted that way in similar cases in other social programs. Mr. Speaker, a Bill will be presented to the House in order to implement these measures.
